(글 과는 별개로 갑자기 드는 생각인데, 펜은 인류에 있어서 최고의 발명품 중 최고이지 않을까. 무언가를 기록할 수 있으니 말이다. 당연한 소리겠지만 기록은 곧 자산이고, 중요한 것을 기록해야 한다.) 영화 의 한 장면으로, 영업하는 사람이라면 한 번쯤은 봤을 영상이다. 이와 비슷하게 물을 팔아보라거나 시가를 팔아보라는 등 무언가를 자신에게 팔아보라고 하는 영상들이 여럿 있다. 이 영상들이 전달하는 메시지는 결국 영업의 본질에 있다. 자기중심적인 사고에서 벗어나 상대방의 입장에서 생각하는 자세, 즉 이기적인 사고에서 타인 중심의 사고로의 전환이다. 이기적의 반댓말은 이타적이지만 이타적이란 단어는 희생이라는 느낌이 더 강하기때문에 타인중심의 사고라는 단어를 썼다. 찾아보니 계몽된 이기주의 라는 단어가 있는데 이게 가장 적합한 것 같다. 다시말해 영업은 내가 무엇을 팔고 싶은지가 아니라 상대방이 무엇을 필요로 하는지부터 생각하는 것이다. 영업은 그렇다치고, 반대의 입장인 소비자로서 지녀야할 행동은 뭘까? 이 소비가 나한테 정녕 합당한지 에 대해서 생각하는 것이 전부다. 요즘은 세상이 극도로 양극화되어가고 있음을 몸소 체감하는 바이다. 인터넷만 봐도 다음은 끝났고 네이버도 저물어 가고 있으며 결국에는 이 트래픽은 구글과 메타가 점령했다고 볼 수 있다. 이제 이 위에 올라설려고 하는 기업이 바로 AI 기업들이다. 이처럼 극단적 기업중심으로 흘러가는 분위기 속에서 도태되거나 동화되거나 둘 중 하나다. 결국에는 AI 기업은 OpenAI 나 Claude, 더 나아가서 국가 차원에서는 미국과 중국 이렇게 양극화 될 것 같다. 대체적으로 기업들은 우리가 무엇을 필요로 하는지 잘 알고 있다. 반면에 정부는 알면서도 묵인하는 경우가 있다. 소비자와 기업은 명백히 상호 이익에 기반한 호혜적 관계라고 할 수 있다. 그렇다면 국가와 국민의 관계는 어떠한가??

title: Optimistic Pessimism Always Wins
description: Hope for the best, prepare for the worst
content: https://youtu.be/l oCt441 E I always emphasize the importance of metacognition in life and try to look at myself objectively, but lately that hasn't been going well. I don't know exactly why, but I can feel the gaps between people widening, and problems that once seemed vague are becoming real. With the arrival of the AI era, I spend a lot of time wondering what I should do next. AI will keep advancing, and I'm afraid that if something I start is eventually replaced by AI, all the time and effort I put into it might feel pointless. I actively use AI myself, so I'm grateful to be living in this era. Yet there is also a vague fear. I agree with the many articles and arguments that AI could threaten humanity, but I also agree with those who say it will benefit the world. Perhaps that looks contradictory. Even outside AI, I seem to hold a lot of contradictory thoughts and attitudes. My desire to avoid conflict with people whenever possible may be one reason. People who are overly positive also put me off. On the other hand, I don't want to deal with overly negative people either. Maybe I'm tired of the world's extreme tendency to split into opposing camps, but I've been living with a simple ' let's keep things agreeable ' attitude. You can see it in the way I tell people not to invest in stocks or crypto, while continuing to invest myself. I'm optimistic about crypto's future. But at the same time, I'm pessimistic. Perhaps I'm closer to an optimistic pessimist than either an optimist or a pessimist. "Hope for the best, prepare for the worst" Expect the best, but be ready for the worst. I don't know how the future will change. I just want to be someone who is optimistic without letting their guard down, and pessimistic without giving up.

title: Preparing for IELTS (edX Courses, Anki, Engnovate, IELTS Bro, Podcasts…)
description: Notes written while preparing for the IELTS test
content: I have taken IELTS before. I attended an academy for a month? Two months? But I remember the result being terrible… (An email recently reminding me that my score would soon expire brought it back to mind.) When deciding to study for an English test again, I debated CELPIP versus IELTS and eventually came full circle and decided to prepare for IELTS once more. These are my personal reasons for choosing IELTS over CELPIP: 1. CELPIP does not have many study materials. 2. I have often heard that if you want to study English properly, you should master IELTS. Aside from those two points, many reviews say that getting a good score on CELPIP is easier and that it is cheaper. I think it is best to choose whichever approach suits you and start studying quickly. IELTS IELTS is an internationally recognized English proficiency test widely used for university and graduate school admission, employment, and immigration in English speaking countries . IELTS is jointly operated by the British Council in the UK, IDP Education in Australia, and Cambridge University Press & Assessment. Registration is mainly handled through the British Council or IDP, and both organizations use the same test difficulty and scoring criteria. You can therefore choose by comparing venue locations, dates, fees, and available study materials. Depending on your purpose, the test is divided into IELTS Academic and IELTS General Training . Both assess Listening, Reading, Writing, and Speaking. Listening and Speaking use the same tests, but Reading and Writing differ in content. Generally, choose Academic when preparing for university or graduate school admission, and General Training when applying for Canadian permanent residence. The fee is approximately KRW 340,000 in Korea and CAD $362–389 in Vancouver, depending on the venue and test format. Results are generally valid for two years from the test date. IELTS Structure and Question Types by Section Listening Test duration Approximately 30 minutes Paper based: 10 minutes to transfer answers Computer delivered: 2 minutes to review answers Test structure: 4 Parts (40 Questions) Social Conversation — Two speakers Social Monologue — One speaker Academic Discussion — Two to four speakers Academic Lecture — One speaker Question types: 7 Question tpyes Form / notes / flowchart Multiple choice Short answer Sentence completion Labelling diagram / map Classification Matching Speaking One on one format, 3 parts, 11–14 minutes Part 1 — Introduction & Interview (4–5 min) Identity check, questions about familiar topics (home, work, studies, hobbies). Part 2 — Individual Long Turn (3–4 min) Task card with a topic and prompts, 1 minute to prepare and make notes, 1–2 minutes to speak, possible follow up questions Part 3 — Discussion (4–5 min) More abstract questions related to Part 2, including opinions, comparisons, and explanations. Assessment criteria Fluency and coherence Lexical resource Grammatical range and accuracy Pronunciation Reading Writing Aiming for Canadian Permanent Residence? To reach CLB 10, the level that earns the maximum language points for permanent residence, you need Reading 8, Writing 7.5, Listening 8.5, and Speaking 7.5 . This is roughly an overall band of 8.0—a score you could describe as allowing only two or three mistakes in each section… Let’s try to achieve as high a score as possible… Study Materials https://takeielts.britishcouncil.org/ https://ielts.idp.com/ https://www.edx.org/learn/test prep/the university of queensland ielts academic test preparation https://ankiweb.net/ https://engnovate.com/ielts tests/ https://ieltsbro.com/ https://www.youtube.com/@EnglishProTips https://open.spotify.com/show/5ISJgLQXgXRzeumkV4eR40

title: Why I Blog
description: Lately, I’ve been collecting posts scattered across different places and moving them to this blog. They were on Notion, WordPress, and Tistory. I also have posts on Facebook, but they feel different in nature, so I haven’t moved those…
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, source: OGQ Lately, I've been collecting posts scattered across different places and moving them to this blog. They were on Notion, WordPress, and Tistory. I also have various posts on Facebook, but they feel different in nature, so I haven't moved those. Having used several blogging platforms, I've come to think Naver Blog is a reasonably good all round option. (I don't know. Ultimately, I think having a blog of my own would be ideal... haha.) Rereading my old posts as I moved them brought back a lot of feelings. I deleted an account at one point, so plenty of posts must have disappeared, but I probably first started blogging as a side hustle. Back when people said you could earn an extra 1 million won a month on Naver Blog, many bloggers got started for that reason, so most probably began much as I did. There was a period when I blogged diligently, but it didn't last long. I think I drifted through different blogging platforms, repeatedly shelving and reviving that dream of a million won a month. I can say with confidence that blogging offers more advantages than disadvantages. For starters, you get free storage. A blog is different from social media. Facebook and X have definitely helped me. My online activity led to offline connections, which helped me find work and build my reputation. I call it luck, but looking back, perhaps it wasn't. I can also say it happened because I posted publicly in public spaces and shared quality writing. That's why most of my posts are public, and I usually leave comments publicly too. If social media is a place to exchange information and communicate, I see blogging as leaning more toward providing information in one direction. All I can do today, too, is hope the algorithm delivers my writing to someone. I don't know whether it's because Naver has become more advertising focused or because there are more AI written posts, but Naver Blog is increasingly commercialized and flooded with posts from fake accounts. Since introducing its "AI Briefing" feature, it has even been openly encouraging AI writing. According to Naver's AI, NAEO, my blog falls below its standards. Apparently I wasn't chosen by Naver's AI... I imagine it gave me a low score because I mainly post personal thoughts rather than informative pieces, and because I focus on text rather than images. Its evaluation criteria include "organizing information with photos/tables" and "comparisons/alternative options," which make me wonder: aren't those things AI does better? What's more, the thumbnail images and tables it recommended are all mass produced AI content. It feels as though it's openly pressuring me to use AI to write useful posts, and I don't like that. We live in a time when AI even codes for us. Now, opening an IDE and writing code yourself seems old fashioned and surprises people. Writing code by hand on paper has become something romantic. Perhaps someday writing blog posts yourself will seem old fashioned too, and picking up a pen to write a diary will remain only as a romantic gesture. Maybe the only way to survive on a blog like this, and keep myself interested, is to use it more like social media. I should communicate more. My interests are money, technology, and news from Canada.

title: Who Is Behind the Web We Use?
description: The invisible order of the web
content: An organization above another organization, and another above that. We live in a system of visible organizations intertwined with layers of invisible order. That system is woven deeply into our daily lives. Even today, when historical status systems have been abolished and equality is taken for granted, hierarchies between people and organizations have not disappeared. A company, for example, has teams, departments, and executives. A country also has many institutions with different powers and responsibilities. The same kind of system exists online. Behind the websites we use without much thought are the people who develop and operate them. Behind those people are the teams building browsers and communications technologies, along with organizations creating standards so different technologies can work together. As users, we may not know what technologies are being used or what happens behind the scenes, yet we enjoy many benefits. And for free, too. That is a wonderful thing. I do not know how far up the web’s hierarchy goes, but I decided to write this post to explore as high as I could. W3C https://www.w3.org/ WHATWG https://whatwg.org/ Ecma https://ecma international.org IETF https://www.ietf.org/ ICANN https://www.icann.org/en The five organizations above are prominent examples of bodies playing important roles in the standards and operating systems of the web and internet. Many other organizations work in their respective fields, collaborating to make different technologies compatible and advance them. Below are related organizations active in those fields (Introduced by AI). Internet Society — ISOC: A nonprofit that promotes the internet’s openness, accessibility, and security. Unicode Consortium: An organization developing standards for characters, emoji, and internationalization. IEEE Standards Association: An organization developing a broad range of technology standards, including Ethernet and wireless LAN. Khronos Group: An organization developing graphics and computing standards such as WebGL, Vulkan, and glTF. FIDO Alliance: An organization developing specifications for secure user authentication, including passkeys. OWASP Foundation: A nonprofit foundation providing application security guidance, verification standards, and tools. Electronic Frontier Foundation — EFF: An organization protecting digital rights such as online privacy and freedom of expression. Tor Project: A nonprofit developing anonymous communications and privacy protection technologies. Mozilla Foundation: A nonprofit foundation pursuing public interest work for an open and fair internet. Open Web Advocacy — OWA: An organization advocating openness and fair competition for browsers and web apps. OpenJS Foundation: A foundation supporting the development and operation of JavaScript and web open source projects. Linux Foundation: A nonprofit foundation supporting Linux, other open source projects, and technological collaboration. Cloud Native Computing Foundation — CNCF: An organization supporting cloud native open source such as Kubernetes and Prometheus. Apache Software Foundation: A nonprofit foundation supporting the operation and communities of Apache open source projects. Free Software Foundation — FSF: A foundation advocating the freedom to use, study, modify, and share software, and supporting GNU and the GPL. Open Source Initiative — OSI: An organization maintaining the Open Source Definition and reviewing and approving open source licenses. Open Source Security Foundation — OpenSSF: A collaborative organization strengthening the security of open source and the software supply chain. Eclipse Foundation: A nonprofit foundation supporting various open source projects, including Eclipse IDE and Jakarta EE. Python Software Foundation — PSF: A nonprofit foundation supporting the Python ecosystem, PyPI, and the developer community. Software Freedom Conservancy — SFC: A nonprofit providing financial, legal, and administrative support to free and open source projects. x402 Foundation: An organization in the Linux Foundation ecosystem supporting the development and adoption of the HTTP based x402 payment protocol. OpenSats: A nonprofit funding developers of free and open source technologies such as Bitcoin and Nostr. Brink: An organization supporting Bitcoin protocol developers through research, education, and mentoring. Reason Foundation: A nonprofit foundation conducting policy research and journalism based on libertarian principles. Cato Institute: A libertarian policy institute advocating individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.

title: Why Does It Feel Like This Moment Will Last Forever?
description: Let me write down my personal thoughts on AI lately.
content: Maybe it will last forever. [\[MUSE ON 2021\] LIVE / Redoor – Forever Has Always Been](https://youtu.be/JNy pVfs6yQ?si=KWSnFYls6x1dQoWW) Let me write down my personal thoughts on AI lately. What computers do best is repetition. That thought hasn't changed. The areas where AI is probably used most are writing, video editing, making songs, and vibe coding. Previously, only people with expertise knew how to create content and use the tools, but AI has broken down that barrier. This means anyone can more easily become a developer, writer, creator, or director—or even try starting a business. Professional domains such as law, medicine, and the judiciary still exist. I see that as the power of a license, and it shows why universities and qualifying exams matter. Even so, we've reached an era when these, too, could someday be replaced. There are invisible connections among us, such as professional networks, personal connections, and closeness. Beyond that, sometimes we look at someone and get an uneasy feeling. We call that intuition or a hunch. Sight = seeing Hearing = listening Smell = smelling Taste = tasting Touch = touching We now need something beyond the five senses—something we might call a sixth sense. AI will dominate activities involving sight and hearing. Through creative works that stimulate those senses, it reaches into our brains. Even my tastes are partly the result of algorithms. Lately, I feel put off when I see AI generated writing and videos. But that isn't true of everything. As a dog owner, I can't easily scroll past a video featuring a cute dog. For now, smell, taste, and touch still seem to be areas machines cannot replace. I have to experience those three senses myself. That's why I think we're in an era when experience matters more. But if we can someday experience them remotely and physically feel them, I wonder whether every human domain will be taken away. The release of Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dot made me feel that we're entering a period when the way we use the web is changing. Honestly, AI can now handle most of what we do online. I suspect this latest AI update will bring more layoffs and fewer junior hires. I realized that the frightening thing about large companies is their ability to wipe out many other businesses at once. Even so, what should we do? Unless AI stops advancing, all we can do is retire or become liars. If we don't voluntarily retire, our options are already set: promote things to people who still don't know this field, or prepare for whatever might happen. As beneficiaries of the AI era, we need to keep following developments and race to become number one in some field that feels like a land grab. The moment something starts doing well, everyone rushes in and copies it. Then the trend changes in an instant. Nothing lasts forever, and we have to move quickly. That's all there is to it.

title: Cookies
description: While browsing websites, we often click “Accept” without thinking when asked, “Do you consent to cookies?” Yet we may not know what cookies actually are. Today, I want to learn about them.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ While browsing websites, we often click “Accept” without thinking when asked, “Do you consent to cookies?” Yet we may not know what cookies actually are. Today, I want to learn about them. The name cookie comes from “magic cookie%EC%9D%B4%ED%9B%84 ).” A cookie is a small text file that a website stores in a user’s browser . Cookies are used for user identification, keeping users logged in, personalization settings, shopping cart functions, and storing browsing history and behavioral tracking information . Simply put, cookies help ensure an efficient and secure web experience. To view cookies in a browser, go to Developer Tools Storage Cookies. You can also enter document.cookie in Developer Tools Console. Developer Tools Network lets you inspect the flow of cookies, too. The actual cookies can be found in database form within the browser’s installation directory. https://support.mozilla.org/en US/kb/about your important data and their files?utm\ source=chatgpt.com About your important data and their files | Firefox Help As the screenshot above shows, cookies have attributes including Name, Value, Domain, Path, Expires/Max Age, HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite . Among these, HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from directly reading or modifying authentication cookies. Secure restricts transmission to HTTPS connections and is practically essential. SameSite limits cookies being attached to requests initiated from other sites, reducing CSRF risk. SameSite=Lax is common. Strict is more restrictive but can affect login flows when arriving via external links. The most commonly used cookies are probably \ ga (GA4) and \ cf\ bm (Cloudflare). Cookies also remember settings such as dark mode and language. For these, HttpOnly should not be applied, and Domain should be limited to the necessary scope. There are different types of cookies, too. Session cookie: A cookie without Expires/Max Age. It is normally deleted when the browser session ends, though it may return when the session is restored. Persistent cookie: A cookie with an expiration condition that may remain after the browser closes. Authentication cookie: Used to authenticate a logged in user. Tracking cookie: Used to track or analyze visits and behavior. First party cookie: Used in the same site context as the site currently being visited. Third party cookie: A cookie belonging to a site other than the one currently being visited, used for advertising, embedded services, and similar purposes. Zombie cookie: A cookie that is recreated after deletion using information left in other storage locations. Cookies can be categorized by how long they last, their purpose, and their relationship to the site. A single cookie that keeps someone logged in may simultaneously be a persistent cookie, an authentication cookie, and a first party cookie. https://www.cloudflare.com/ko kr/learning/privacy/what are cookies/ What are cookies? | Cookie definition Let’s use an example to make this easier to understand. Imagine the frontend as a restaurant’s dining room, where customers are welcomed, and the backend as the kitchen, where orders are handled. The restaurant needs to remember each customer’s order and requests. As more customers arrive, it becomes harder to distinguish who ordered what, so each customer receives a numbered ticket. When a customer places an additional order, they show the ticket, and the restaurant finds the order record for that number and continues processing it. Session management using cookies is similar. The session ID cookie kept in the browser is the customer’s ticket, while the session data stored on the server is the restaurant’s order record. A cookie may contain only a number, or it may directly contain simple settings such as dark mode or language. The example above might make cookies sound like something used for marketing. It is true that cookies are used for marketing today. But the original purpose of web cookies was to maintain state—such as a shopping cart—between otherwise independent HTTP requests. Over time, Memcached and Redis came to be used to store server side session data and let several servers access the same records. In restaurant terms, this is an order management system that several kitchens can consult together. Wherever the records are stored, however, the restaurant still needs to identify which customer a request belongs to. Cookies and these storage systems can therefore be used together. Cookie consent laws differ by country, so services must inform users about cookie use and obtain any required consent according to the laws that apply and the purposes for which the cookies are used.

title: Sin Tax, Pigouvian Tax, and Windfall Tax
description: Governments collect taxes to cover the shared costs of keeping a country functioning safely and enabling its people to live well together. The basic purpose is similar everywhere, but the types and characteristics of taxes differ by country. Today, I want to explore some unusual taxes…
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ What is the real reason we pay taxes? Governments collect taxes to cover the shared costs of keeping a country functioning safely and enabling all its people to live well together. The basic purpose of tax revenue is the same across countries, but the types and characteristics of taxes differ. Today, I want to look at some rather unusual taxes. 1\. Sin tax: A particularly high tax imposed on consumption considered socially harmful or undesirable. Typical examples include tobacco, alcohol, gambling, cannabis, and sugary drinks. The purpose of a sin tax is to discourage certain consumption, with a focus on reducing services that negatively affect society or consumption deemed undesirable. Apparently, there have also been cases of taxes on prostitution and the sex trade in the past. Looking at the composition of sin taxes collected in Korea, tobacco taxes account for 70%, alcohol/liquor taxes for over 20%, and the remainder comes from gambling industries such as casinos, horse racing, and lotteries. On a KRW 4,500 pack of cigarettes, taxes and levies amount to 74% (KRW 3,233): tobacco consumption tax, the National Health Promotion levy, individual consumption tax, local education tax, value added tax, and other charges. Someone smoking a pack a day is a taxpayer contributing over KRW 1 million a year through cigarettes alone. As a nonsmoker, I can agree with raising cigarette prices and collecting taxes. But if prices rise to an absurd level and smokers quit, reducing revenue, the government will collect that money elsewhere. So I cannot say it is entirely a good thing. On the other hand, cigarettes dirty the streets and damage health, so I cannot simply encourage smoking either. Perhaps the e cigarette industry could offer a somewhat reasonable compromise. 2\. Pigouvian tax: A tax created to address environmental problems. 3\. Windfall tax: A tax policy applying only to companies, imposing an additional tax on excess profits when they earn unexpectedly large gains because of external circumstances rather than special efforts or improvements in productivity. Taxes are an important mechanism that allows society to function properly. As the saying goes, “Nothing is certain except death and taxes.” Taxes are inseparable from our lives and a central source of funding for running a country. But when you look at different taxes one by one, some seem unusual or difficult to understand intuitively from an ordinary person’s perspective. As taxpaying members of a country, it is natural for us to care about the criteria used to collect taxes and where the money goes. The government, too, has a responsibility to use taxpayers’ money reasonably and disclose both the process and the results transparently. Still, even if a tax serves a good purpose, I do not think the government needs to intervene excessively in the market. That may sound contradictory, but no matter how I think about it, I have seen far more examples of taxes being used badly than well. So much is wasted on incomprehensible spending, corruption, misconduct, and abuses of authority. (The Yeosu Island Expo, the Saemangeum Jamboree, KRW 5 trillion in financial incentives for Gwangju…) Conclusion: Whoever invented sin taxes is the real worst of the worst… Taxes SinTax PigouvianTax WindfallTax

title: Understanding Interest Rates and Bonds
description: For example, if you borrow KRW 1 million for one year at 5% per annum, the simple interest rate is 5% and the interest amount is KRW 50,000.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ “Rate = Interest rate” Interest = An amount of money For example, if you borrow KRW 1 million for one year at 5% per annum, the simple interest rate is 5% and the interest amount is KRW 50,000. Ways of calculating interest \ Simple interest = Interest is charged only on the principal. \ Compound interest = Interest is charged again on the principal plus accumulated interest. Interest rates apply both when lending money and when borrowing it. When the news reports a rate hike, it usually refers to the central bank’s policy rate. Why, then, is the central bank’s policy rate important? A bank’s basic earnings structure revolves around “raising funds.” One of a bank’s main functions is to obtain funds and lend them to individuals and businesses that need money . It raises funds through methods such as accepting customer deposits and issuing bonds, then earns the difference between the interest received on loans and the interest paid to obtain those funds. When the central bank’s policy rate rises, the interest banks pay to obtain money generally rises, too. In other words, the chain is Policy rate rises → Interbank lending rates rise → Banks’ funding costs increase → Customer lending rates rise . Higher customer lending rates increase the interest burden on households and businesses. If competition to attract customers’ money is intense, banks may also raise deposit rates. As a result, consumption and investment tend to decline, while asset markets such as real estate and stocks also tend to contract . Trading Economics Let’s look at interest rates by country at the time of writing. The fourth column, “Interest Rate,” shows the rate. The United States is at 4.0% per year, Japan at 1.25%, and Korea at 3.0%. (Decisions to raise, lower, or hold rates are announced eight times a year, once every six to seven weeks.) Naver deposit and installment savings comparison I was not around in the 1970s and 1980s, so I cannot speak from experience, but older people say interest rates exceeded 20% back then… I do not know how long that lasted. That may be why older people tell us to put money steadily into the bank rather than invest in stocks. In any case, when opening a deposit, installment savings account, or cash parking account, choose one with a higher rate. These days, there are plenty of special offers and preferential rates, so I hope you compare them carefully and choose wisely. After all, a well managed savings ladder can also provide stable returns. Bonds are also closely linked to interest rates. “Debt = Money owed” “Claim = The right to receive money” “Creditor = The person entitled to receive money” “Debtor = The person who must repay money” “Credit = The extent to which someone can be trusted to repay money” “Collateral = An asset pledged so it can be taken if the borrower fails to repay” “Default = Failure to repay principal or interest as promised” Example: I borrow KRW 100 million from a bank at 5% per year for three years and pledge a car as collateral. (Principal repaid in full at maturity.) Debtor = Me Creditor = The bank Principal = KRW 100 million Interest rate = 5% per year Interest = KRW 416,667 × 36 months Maturity = Three years Collateral = The car The example above involves bank lending and credit. Another area is the bond market , where debt and bonds are traded. Depending on the issuer, bonds include government bonds / municipal bonds / corporate bonds / financial bonds / agency bonds . Bond = Debt made into a security Face value (Coupon) = The regular interest promised by a bond Maturity = When the principal is repaid Yield = The return an investor earns based on the current price Example: To raise KRW 100 million, the government issues a three year government bond paying 3% annually. Debtor = The government Creditor = The government bond investor Principal = KRW 100 million Coupon rate = 3% per year Interest = KRW 3 million per year Maturity = Three years New government bonds may be issued as existing bonds approach maturity, or because the government actually needs funds. This also means the government continues adding debt. Ultimately, we need to look at who is buying those government bonds. Understanding interest rates and government bonds is complicated in many ways… \ Policy rate ↑ → Existing bond prices ↓ → Bond yields ↑ \ Policy rate ↓ → Existing bond prices ↑ → Bond yields ↓ \ People sell bonds → Bond prices ↓ → Yield ↑ \ People buy bonds → Bond prices ↑ → Yield ↓ These relationships have been treated almost like formulas in markets to date. Taking this further, one may also see the chain as “Inflation ↑ → Expectations of rate hikes ↑ → Government bond yields ↑ → Bond prices ↓ → Discount rates ↑ → Pressure on stock valuations.” Bonds Stocks Deposits InstallmentSavings Interest Banks Credit

title: How to Definitely Make Money from a Blog
description: Before starting a blog, you’ve probably imagined writing, earning money, getting advertising offers, and working hard at it as a side hustle. You may have searched for monetized blogs, decorated yours, and tried to post consistently. Anyone who has blogged knows it isn’t easy…
content: Not easy. Before starting a blog, you've probably imagined it at least once: writing posts, making money, getting advertising offers, and working hard at it as a side hustle. You may have searched for monetized blogs, decorated your own, and tried to write consistently. Anyone who has ever blogged knows it isn't easy. So I'm writing this to organize my thoughts on how we should approach blogging. 1\. Write about things other people are curious about, rather than simply what you want to write. The hardest thing about starting a blog is having to write without knowing who your readers are. You need to think carefully about the tone and level of your writing. If you want a topic that most people will be curious about regardless of who they are, write something timely. 2\. However, timely posts can become buried as time passes. If views are your main focus, writing breaking news style posts may be useful, but you'll soon wear yourself out. Writing becomes tiring and exhausting, making it hard to keep going for long. And because anyone can run this kind of labor intensive blog, it's not easy to survive. 3\. Even so, it's worth continually thinking about which topics are timely and likely to attract interest. If you find something you feel capable of writing about, use the knowledge you have to produce a thoughtful post quickly. 4\. As you steadily accumulate good posts, there will eventually be a moment when one ranks highly in search results or gets shared and takes off. While waiting for that moment, keep stocking your blog with good writing. That's why the most important part of blogging is to keep writing consistently at a reasonable level of quality. 5\. I think the era of making money purely from blog views has passed. Of course, some people still do, but aiming to earn from page views when you're just starting is a somewhat old fashioned approach to running a blog. 6\. Use your blog to build a brand around yourself. You can learn a lot in the process: what topics people care about, how they search before finding you, why your own view counts are low, and so on. Only when you seriously think about your blog can you begin to grow. 7\. Rather than just writing posts, I'm thinking about where to put them so people will actually see them. With Google search acting strangely these days, I've been wondering how to get my posts near the top of its results. 8\. Tistory definitely has a very different atmosphere from Naver. People don't build friendships by adding blog neighbors, and there are fewer topic categories showcasing Tistory posts than on Naver. 9\. The usual advice for creating an optimized blog is to choose one topic and upload only content related to it, but I'm not sure that works on Tistory. (If the aim is maximum exposure, wouldn't it make more sense to write quickly, regardless of the topic...?) Posts need to be easy to read and coherent while attracting as much attention as possible. 10\. Coming back to the topic, here's how to definitely make money from a blog: 1) write things people will find interesting, 2) write consistently, 3) steadily collect good posts on your blog, and 4) write timely posts too. Still not making money after all that? Even so, try it for just 100 days, and you'll gain experience worth more than money. 11\. Let's all start blogging. With a Lucky Vicky mindset.

title: [Marriage] Choosing a Wedding Venue or Wedding Hall

content: [\[Marriage\] Choosing a Wedding Date: Auspicious Days in 2027, Peak and Off Peak Seasons, and Holidays](https://blog.naver.com/martin lee/224391813548) Once you have chosen your wedding date, you need to choose a venue. Wedding venues usually start taking bookings one year before the wedding. The places you saw on Instagram and thought, “ Wow, this is beautiful. I have to get married here! ” or venues so famous that everyone knows their names may already be fully booked even if you inquire a year ahead. So if there is a venue you really want, I recommend keeping in touch well in advance. Before choosing a venue, I think there are four main things to consider. 1\. Budget 2\. Number of guests 3\. Location 4\. Atmosphere It goes without saying that the budget matters most. Wedding venue prices vary enormously because one extra charge leads to another, and then another. That is why I think the couple should start by setting a firm budget for how much they will spend on the wedding. Of course, you may have a dream wedding in mind. It might be a once in a lifetime event. That sounds lovely. But graduation was a once in a lifetime event, too, and you only turned twenty once. When I was in school, I wanted a mobile phone, and my parents said they would buy me one if I got good exam results. I studied hard just because I wanted that phone, and when I finally got my first one, I was thrilled. But that feeling did not last forever. Maybe about seven days after I got it? Anyway, weddings are like that, too. Looking at the reality of weddings in Korea today, I feel they are being given far more significance than we realize. Besides, a wedding is about more than fulfilling a dream. It is also an event for both families' parents. Sometimes more of the parents' acquaintances and relatives attend than the couple's own guests. Before booking a venue, make sure you check the guest count with your parents. That is also why location matters. When choosing a location, check whether transportation is convenient, how many cars can park, and how long guests can park for. Like me, many young people move from other regions to Seoul for work and live there, so many weddings take place in Seoul. Their colleagues and friends are there, too. Since family members travel up from other regions, a location near a train station or bus terminal is generally a good choice. If the guests are somewhat older, many may drive to the venue. In that case, parking is an absolute must. Finally, there is the atmosphere you want for your wedding. The three points above are actually easier because you can assess them objectively. Atmosphere, however, depends on personal taste, so it helps to decide on the style you want. 1\. Hotel wedding 2\. Wedding hall 3\. House wedding or small wedding 4\. Garden or outdoor venue 5\. Hanok or traditional venue 6\. Chapel or cathedral style venue 7\. Restaurant or dining wedding And so on... There is a huge range. Even conventional wedding halls differ depending on whether they have a bright or dark atmosphere, high or low ceilings, and a long or short wedding aisle. All of that changes how the space feels. That is what makes it difficult. Flowers can especially transform the atmosphere of hotel, outdoor, and hanok weddings. If you do not know what you like, try using the following prompts to help. A. Grand and classic → High ceilings, a long wedding aisle, chandeliers, a cathedral or hotel feel B. Warm and charming → A house wedding, a small space, and a relaxed atmosphere with guests close by C. Natural and bright → Outdoors, gardens, full height windows, natural light, and plenty of greenery D. Korean and refined → Hanok, historic homes, traditional architecture, and an atmosphere that also suits hanbok Touring actual wedding venues would be best. content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ I happened to see an Instagram video discussing serious literacy problems among younger generations, and it struck a nerve. I waste many hours on social media every day. Perhaps that is why I sometimes feel my own reading comprehension declining. I have developed a habit of speaking with all purpose pronouns such as “this,” “that,” and “that thing.” My speech is losing its logical structure, and longer pieces are becoming harder to read. Media organizations and newspapers develop identities shaped by the political circumstances of their founding. They inevitably carry historical, economic, social, and political leanings. In other words, it is important to subscribe to outlets whose values fit your own. Writing has an invisible but formidable power. title: [Notice] Why Overseas Koreans Complain So Damn Much About Korea
description: Living in Vancouver, which has a relatively large Korean population even by Canadian standards…
content: https://faceeast.substack.com/p/5a8?r=4iguvd&utm\ campaign=post expanded share&utm\ medium=post%20viewer Why Overseas Koreans Complain So Damn Much About Korea I wouldn't quite call myself a diaspora Korean, but... This post really resonates with me. Living in Vancouver, which has a relatively large Korean population even by Canadian standards, I hear about Koreans behaving badly, and there's usually at least one Korean wherever I go. In many ways, it isn't that different from Korea. All my news about Korea comes from stories posted in Korean community groups or on social media. That's why life seems more peaceful if you stay away from Korean community forums as much as possible. There's far too much unnecessary gossip. At least writing your own thoughts on Naver Blog seems like the healthiest option. Anyway, at a time like this, when Korea's international standing is rising, I think a strange mixture of emotions comes up. There's the hope that choosing to live abroad was a better decision than staying in Korea. At the same time, I wonder, "Am I here for no reason?" or "Was my choice a mistake?" Some people really are considering moving back. But we've already spent time here, and the prospect of going back to Korea and starting over is frightening. So I sometimes see people justify their choice by saying, "That's just how Korea is," "Korea is a hard place to live," or "Korea is still an old fashioned society obsessed with age." Meanwhile, they deliberately look away from Canada's problems. In Korea, when someone's thinking leans too far in one direction, people say they've become left wing or right wing. Looking at this, I sometimes joke that they've become Canada wing. I'm not trying to put Korea on a pedestal. Viewed objectively, it is unquestionably a very good country. https://www.asiatoday.co.kr/kn/view.php?key=20260916010006087 If you disagree, I wonder whether it's because you didn't live in Seoul. Among people who immigrate to Vancouver, there seem to be far more from outside the Seoul–Gyeonggi area, so perhaps their view makes sense. Of course, some came because they were exhausted from working endlessly and pushing themselves so hard in Korea, and wanted a more relaxed, family centered life. Others wanted overseas experience. Whether people immigrated or moved for their own personal circumstances, or even as a form of escape, I think focusing on the present is the right and mature thing to do, whatever the reason. We weren't dragged here against our will; we chose this country voluntarily. More than anything, it depends on our own mindset. I hope we take responsibility and live happily with a positive outlook. But rather than trying to feel superior by putting someone else down, let's give credit where it's due. If something is wrong, we should say it's wrong. Many people say they're living much better lives in Canada than they did in Korea. That's wonderful. It's something to congratulate them on. But people whose lives became worse can naturally return to Korea, so of course we don't see as many of them here. It's difficult to admit that your judgment was wrong. It seems to get harder as you get older. That's stubbornness. Every country has good and bad points, and the choices I've made can change at any time. Coming to Canada doesn't mean I have to live here forever, and returning to Korea doesn't mean I've failed. If you were wrong, you can change course. What we need more of as we age is principles, not stubbornness. Keep your thinking flexible and your convictions firm.

content: AI may do all the coding these days, but I am taking CS50. I explained why in this post. Week 1 Scratch Week 2 C Week 3 Arrays Week 4 Algorithms Week 5 Memory Week 6 Data Structures … The difficulty suddenly increased in week 5. So this time, I want to write a post reviewing and organizing what I have learned so far. Variables The name of a space used to store a value is called a “variable.” int, string, float, double, char, and bool are types. A const value that does not change is called a “constant.” Conditionals if else if else Loops for while do while Functions input → \[ “function” \] → output Likewise, in a computer: source code → \[ “compiler” \] → machine code C C does not have a type called string. “char \ variable name” is the correct form. The command make filename means clang "filename.c" o "program\ name" l "libraryname". In C, main(int argc, char \ argv\[\]) means that the program receives arguments entered alongside its invocation (./filename). int main(void) means there is no return value. A return statement is not required. return 0 means normal completion; return 1 means an error. A function’s prototype must be declared before using it. “sizeof” tells you how many bytes a type uses. Ampersand (&) Asterisk (\ ) malloc, realloc, free Pass by value: By default, a value is copied and passed to a function. struct groups several pieces of data into one type. typedef struct p; can be used like p.name ="martin", p.age=22;. Arrays int number\[3\]; Array indexes start at 0. An array stores values of the same data type. A string is represented as a char array, ending with “NULL (\\0).” Arrays are stored contiguously in memory. In most situations, an array name is converted into something like a pointer to its first element. Algorithms 1\. Linear Search: Check each item one by one from the beginning. O(n) 2\. Binary Search: Check the middle value in a sorted array. O(log n) Big O, from fastest: O(1) O(log n) O(n) O(n log n) O(n^2) 3\. Selection Sort: Find the smallest value and place it at the front. O(n^2) 4\. Bubble Sort: Compare adjacent values and move the larger one toward the end. O(n^2) 5\. Merge Sort: Keep dividing the array in half, then merge the parts while sorting them. O(n log n) To be continued…

title: What Exactly Is the Middle East?
description: Where is the Middle East?
content: Where is the Middle East? When we hear “the Middle East,” places that produce oil readily come to mind. Usually, Western Asia and the area around Egypt are grouped together as the Middle East. The countries and territories include: Saudi Arabia UAE Qatar Kuwait Bahrain Oman Yemen Iraq Iran Israel Jordan Lebanon Syria The Palestinian territories Turkey Egypt These are grouped together as the Middle East. If the scope is broadened to include North Africa, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco are sometimes also considered part of the Middle East. Why the Middle East Matters 1\. Resources 2\. title: Types of Income
description: Income categories follow Korea’s Income Tax Act.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ Income categories follow the Income Tax Act . An individual’s income is classified into eight categories. Corporations have a separate Corporate Tax Act. There are also the Value Added Tax Act, Inheritance Tax and Gift Tax Act, Local Tax Act, and various other tax laws. For now, let’s start with personal income. 1\. Interest income: Money received in exchange for providing your money to others (interest from deposits, installment savings, bonds, etc.). 2\. Dividend income: Income received in return for investing in a company’s capital (dividends and distributions). 3\. Business income: Income generated by continuously and repeatedly carrying on a business. 3.3% = Income tax of 3% + Local income tax of 0.3% 4\. Employment income: Income received for providing labor under an employment relationship (monthly salary, annual salary, bonuses, performance pay, etc.). Tax already deducted when you receive your salary is withholding tax. Recalculating the exact amount at year end is the year end tax settlement. 5\. Pension income: Money received as a pension (National Pension, civil service pensions, private school teachers’ pensions, military pensions, pension savings, and certain IRP pension payments). 6\. Other income: Specific types of income defined in the Income Tax Act. \ Prize money \ Bounties \ Rewards \ Occasional lecture fees \ Manuscript fees \ Certain royalties \ Honoraria \ Compensation for services provided on a one off basis \ Religious workers’ income (\ Whether an activity is continuous and repeated is the most important factor in determining the category.) The six categories above are collectively called comprehensive income. (Comprehensive income tax) The remaining categories—7. Retirement income and 8. Capital gains—are called separately assessed income. 7\. Retirement income: Money received upon retirement (retirement/severance pay). 8\. Capital gains (capital gains tax): Income generated by transferring ownership of assets. \ Land \ Buildings \ Apartments \ Presale rights \ Rights relating to real estate \ Certain shares \ Other assets specified by law When we sell assets like these, we must pay capital gains tax. Interest and dividend income are generally taxed at 15.4%. Business and employment income: Korea’s basic comprehensive income tax rates are divided into eight progressive brackets, ranging from 6% to 45%, depending on taxable income. Taxable income Income tax rate Up to KRW 14 million 6% Over KRW 14 million to KRW 50 million 15% Over KRW 50 million to KRW 88 million 24% Over KRW 88 million to KRW 150 million 35% Over KRW 150 million to KRW 300 million 38% Over KRW 300 million to KRW 500 million 40% Over KRW 500 million to KRW 1 billion 42% Over KRW 1 billion 45% The important point is this: If your annual salary is KRW 100 million, you do not pay 35% on the entire KRW 100 million. It is a progressive tax , with 6%, 15%, 24%, and 35% applied successively to the respective brackets. And individual local income tax is generally added separately at 10% of the income tax amount. In practice, the combined rates are approximately 6.6%, 16.5%, 26.4%, 38.5% … up to 49.5%. For pension income, the rate varies by age and pension type. Other income is basically taxed at 20% + 2%. Retirement income and capital gains are calculated separately. Capital gains can be taxed at up to 70%, making this one of the more complicated areas. TypesOfIncome ComprehensiveIncomeTax Income

title: [React Native] What Is Metro?
description: React Native uses a bundler called Metro.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ https://reactnative.dev/docs/metro Metro · React Native React Native uses a bundler called Metro. In web terms, it is similar to Vite or Webpack. That is what it does. More specifically: Follow imports to find the required files. Transform code such as TypeScript/JSX into JavaScript. Organize modules into a single executable bundle. Detect code changes during development. Deliver changes to the app for Fast Refresh. Defined as stages: 1\. Resolver: Finds which actual file an import refers to. 2\. Transformer: Converts TS/JSX and similar code into a form the target platform understands. Uses a Babel based transformer by default. 3\. Serializer: Combines the transformed modules to produce the final bundle. https://metrobundler.dev/ Metro Previously, you had to create and modify a metro.config.js file, but these days the @react native/metro config and @expo/metro config packages include Metro’s default configuration. In other words, React Native/Expo and Metro are practically inseparable. (RePack is one technology that can replace Metro, however.) One of the most noticeable Metro changes in RN 0.73 was that symlink support became stable and enabled by default. A symlink (symbolic link) points to a file or folder in another location instead of copying the actual file or folder. Environments such as npm workspaces frequently use this structure to share common packages across several projects. As a result, Metro’s Resolver can follow a symlink’s actual path and recognize shared packages as regular dependencies. Development features such as Fast Refresh also work more naturally with this structure. In other words, Metro’s symlink support in RN 0.73 is better understood as an infrastructure improvement that helps React Native support modern JavaScript project structures—monorepos, workspaces, and shared packages—rather than a change that adds a new app feature. Previously, using shared code from outside a React Native project was tricky. Since RN 0.73, Metro understands symlinks by default, making it much easier to set up several apps that share the same code. In short, Metro = The package that serves as RN’s bundler. title: Canada’s Sovereign Wealth Funds & the Canada Strong Fund
description: I suddenly became curious about Canada’s sovereign wealth funds and decided to look into them and make a record.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ I suddenly became curious about Canada’s sovereign wealth funds and decided to look into them and make a record. The underlying reason was that I had recently read about rebalancing Korea’s National Pension Service investments and wanted to know how Canada manages its system. Korea, Canada, and Japan operate similar pension systems, described as “mandatory, earnings related public pensions” or “social insurance public pensions.” Korea’s National Pension Service (NPS) Salary → National Pension contributions → NPS → Investment → National Pension payments CPP (Canadian Pension Plan) Salary → CPP contributions → CPP Investments → Investment → CPP payments Japan also operates a national pension and an employees’ pension. When you receive a salary, you must contribute a portion of your income to the public pension, which is managed by the national public pension fund. How, then, does this differ from Norway’s sovereign wealth fund , which is widely considered well managed? At first, I thought Canada’s CPP had a structure similar to Norway’s sovereign wealth fund. But after looking into it, I found that although their investment methods share some similarities, their starting points are entirely different. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund began with the idea of “oil → government revenue → investment → assets for future generations.” Rather than spending all the revenue from selling finite resources such as oil and natural gas today, the country converts it into financial assets to leave to future generations. In other words, Norway’s fund is a sovereign wealth fund managing money the country earns from resources , whereas CPP is a public pension managing contributions paid by workers and employers . People may think of CPP Investments as Canada’s sovereign wealth fund, but strictly speaking, it is not one. How big is CPP? $793.3B , or roughly KRW 800 trillion. (Korea’s National Pension is around KRW 1,600 trillion.) CPP is managed in two separate components: Base CPP / Additional CPP . \ Base CPP : Canada’s original basic CPP, which has been operating for years. \ Additional CPP : The enhancement introduced in 2019 to increase the retirement income provided by CPP. It is easier to think of this as an additional layer of pension coverage on top of the existing CPP, rather than two separate national pensions. In Korea, “national pension” immediately brings to mind one enormous institution, NPS. In Canada, however, public funds are spread across several very large investment institutions. \ CPP Investments = National public pension \ PSP Investments = Federal public sector pensions (civil servants, military personnel, RCMP, etc.) \ La Caisse = Québec public institution pensions \ BCI = BC public sector pensions, including civil servants and teachers \ AIMCo = Alberta public pensions + government funds \ Ontario Teachers’ = Ontario teachers’ pension \ Alberta Heritage Fund = Alberta resource revenue fund \ Canada Growth Fund = Federal policy investment fund To see which stocks CPP Investments buys or sells, you can Google “CPP Investments holdings/portfolios” and check its holdings. https://www.koreatimes.net/ArticleViewer/Article/176634 The article above is dated April 27, 2026. Its main point was that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney would establish a new sovereign wealth fund. “Canada Strong Fund” The details have not yet been released, but it looks worth keeping an eye on. title: Financial Statement Analysis Terms to Know
description: When researching a company or reading economic and current-affairs news, unfamiliar terms often come up.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ When researching a company or reading economic and current affairs news, unfamiliar terms often come up. Many sound familiar but are easy to confuse, so I decided to organize them in a post. (Writing this with help from ChatGPT…) I believe I will get used to these terms, too, if I see them often enough. \ Revenue = How much was sold = Total revenue \ Cost of goods sold = The cost of the goods \ Gross profit = Money left from the products themselves = Revenue Cost of goods sold \ Selling, general, and administrative expenses = Company operating expenses (salaries, advertising, rent, travel, etc.) \ Operating profit = Profit earned from the core business \ Operating loss = Negative operating profit \ Profit before tax = Final profit before paying taxes \ Net income = Final profit after accounting for taxes as well \ Net loss = A loss on the bottom line \ Operating profit margin = Operating profit / Revenue \ Net profit margin = Net income / Revenue For example: Revenue of KRW 10 billion → Operating profit of KRW 1 billion → Net income of KRW 600 million . This means the company sold KRW 10 billion worth of goods or services, earned KRW 1 billion from its core business, and ultimately had KRW 600 million left after interest, taxes, and other items . \ Profit/surplus = Money left over \ Loss/deficit = Money lost Operating profit and net income \ Non operating income = Money earned outside the core business \ Non operating expenses = Expenses incurred outside the core business \ Interest income = Interest earned on deposits and similar assets \ Interest expense = Interest on loans and similar obligations \ Foreign exchange gain = Money earned from exchange rate movements \ Foreign exchange loss = Money lost from exchange rate movements \ Foreign currency transaction gain/loss = Gains or losses arising from foreign currency transactions \ Gain on disposal of tangible assets = Profit from selling buildings, machinery, and similar assets \ Gain on disposal of investment assets = Profit from selling investment assets \ Impairment loss = An accounting loss recognizing a significant decline in an asset’s value \ Corporate income tax expense = Income tax paid by a company If operating profit is KRW 3 billion but net income is only KRW 500 million, check whether interest, foreign exchange losses, taxes, or one time losses were large. Conversely, if operating profit is KRW 3 billion but net income is KRW 7 billion, substantial gains may have occurred outside the core business, such as property sales or investment gains. Is the company financially sound? \ Assets = The total economic value a company owns (Liabilities + Equity) \ Liabilities = What the company owes = Debt \ Equity = Assets Liabilities \ Share capital = The basic capital initially invested by shareholders \ Retained earnings = Money accumulated in the company = Accumulated profits \ Debt to equity ratio = Liabilities / Equity \ Equity ratio = Equity / Assets \ Current assets = Assets that can be converted to cash within one year (cash, receivables, inventory, etc.) \ Current liabilities = Liabilities payable within one year = Short term debt \ Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities \ Borrowings = Money borrowed from financial institutions and others = Loans \ Net debt = Borrowings Cash and cash equivalents For example, if a company has KRW 10 billion in assets and KRW 3 billion in debt, its own funds—equity—amount to KRW 7 billion. \ Operating cash flow = \ Investing cash flow = \ Financing cash flow = \ Cash and cash equivalents = \ CAPEX = \ Free cash flow (FCF) = Terms in the news \ Improving/deteriorating results \ Earnings surprise \ Earnings shock \ Turnaround \ Base effect \ One time gains/expenses \ Margin \ Cost to sales ratio \ Leverage \ Deleveraging Terms used in stocks \ Market capitalization = Current share price × Number of shares outstanding \ ROE = Net income relative to equity \ ROA = How much the company earns relative to its total assets \ PER = An indicator showing the multiple of earnings at which a stock trades \ PBR = An indicator showing the multiple of net asset value at which a stock trades \ EPS = Net income per share \ BPS = Net assets per share \ Dividend = A portion of the money a company earns that is distributed to shareholders \ Dividend yield = Dividends as a proportion of the current share price Income statement: A statement showing how much a company sold, how much it spent, and how much it ultimately earned or lost over a period. Balance sheet: A statement showing the assets a company owns, the liabilities it owes, and the equity that is actually its own at a particular point in time. Cash flow statement: A statement showing where cash came from and where it went over a period. Income statement = Does it earn well? Balance sheet = Is it financially solid? Cash flow statement = Is actual cash flowing well? I think that is a useful way to remember them. FinancialStatements Companies Money

title: [Canadian Stocks] Shortlisting ETFs
description: There is a famous investing saying: “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket.”
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ There is a famous investing saying: “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket.” It is another way of saying not to go all in on a single stock. Of course, some stocks, such as Coca Cola, may keep trending upward. But if you had bought Nike instead, the result would have been disastrous. That is why this saying often comes up when discussing diversification to reduce investment risk. Increasing the number of stocks you own is one way to diversify. Buying an ETF is another form of diversification. ETF = Exchange Traded Fund. It is a fund that holds a collection of assets. One of the best known ETFs is QQQ, which invests in 100 U.S. technology stocks. It holds stocks such as Nvidia / Apple / Microsoft / Amazon / Micron … at different weights. Large asset managers such as BlackRock (iShares), Vanguard, and Invesco create and manage ETFs. An ETF’s advantage is that it offers a convenient and safer way to invest in several companies at once. However, since it invests in an entire market or a particular sector, its price falls when that market falls, and returns may be lower than those from individual stocks. Buying several ETFs can also result in overlapping holdings. Let’s look at which ETFs people tend to prefer in Canada. https://www.reddit.com/r/CanadaInvesting/ r/CanadaInvesting There does not seem to be an equivalent to the individual stock discussion boards on Toss or Naver yet. Reddit seems to be the most active option. Preferences may change over time, but from what I have recently seen on Reddit, people seem especially fond of VFV, XEQT, and QQC . To list a few more: VFV = U.S. S&P 500 ($34B) XIC = Canadian total market ($32.9B) XIU = Canada’s 60 large companies ($24.6B) XEQT = Global equities ($21.5B) ZCN = Canadian total market ($18.1B) VCN = Canadian total market ($16.9B) VEQT = Global equities ($16.2B) ZAG = Canadian bonds ($13.1B) VDY = Canadian high dividend stocks ($9.2B) ZEB = Canadian banks ($7.3B) XGRO = 80% stocks + 20% bonds ($5.2B) XUU = U.S. total market ($4.7B) XGD = Global gold miners ($4.0B) QQC = Nasdaq 100 ($3.7B) XEG = Canadian energy ($2.2B) XRE = Canadian REITs ($1.1B) CGL.C = Physical gold (0.77B) XMA = Canadian mining, metals, and fertilizers ($0.71B) If I build a portfolio and plan to add ETFs, I should consider the ones highlighted in green: XIU, VEQT, XGD, XEG, and XMA. ( This is simply because I personally expect Canada to do well. These are absolutely not stock recommendations. ) (I do not particularly like drawing chart lines on indexes, so I have included only the prices.) They have climbed steadily so far, and I do not know when to get in. ETFs seem heavily influenced by the market or sector. So let’s buy regularly in installments. title: Korea’s 2026 Tax Reform Proposal Announced
description: The Ministry of Finance and Economy (formerly the Ministry of Economy and Finance) announces a tax reform proposal every year.
content: The Ministry of Finance and Economy (formerly the Ministry of Economy and Finance) announces a tax reform proposal every year. This year, it announced the 2026 tax reform proposal on August 3. https://www.mofe.go.kr/nw/nes/detailNesDtaView.do?searchBbsId1=MOSFBBS\ 000000000028&searchNttId1=MOSF\ 000000000078809&menuNo=4010100 Ministry of Finance and Economy Tax laws do not change as soon as the proposal is announced. Announcement → Advance legislative notice → Cabinet meeting → Submission of tax amendment bills to the National Assembly → Assembly deliberation and vote → Promulgation → Implementation Tax amendments are finalized through this process. After the provisions that pass the National Assembly are promulgated into law, they apply from the effective dates specified in each law. I would like to read the full detailed PDF of the tax reform proposal, but it is 250 pages long. Below are two government infographics on the 2026 tax reform proposal. Homeowners should probably focus on the real estate sections. For ordinary and upper middle income people like me who do not own a home, the following seem worth paying attention to. 1 3. Supporting productive finance and capital markets — ISA reform 2 1. Support for ordinary and upper middle income households 2 2. Support for young people, marriage, and childbirth 4 1. Rationalizing the tax system: suppressing share prices?? Reading through it made me think I should also study the basics of tax law… The ISA reform includes two elements: “restructuring the general ISA and introducing a productive finance ISA.” An ISA is an account with tax benefits provided by the government to encourage people to build assets and invest for the long term. For ordinary people, it is one of the few remaining ladders to building wealth—a small ray of hope. Net income is tax exempt up to KRW 2 million for the general type and KRW 4 million for the low income and farmer/fisher type , with a lower tax rate also applied to amounts above those limits. Under the existing ISA rules, you could keep extending the account after completing the minimum three year holding period. That meant you could maintain it long term simply by continuing to renew it. But the new proposal would change the general ISA to an initial three years plus a maximum two year extension, allowing only five years in total. There is also a change to contribution limits: “unused annual limits cannot be carried forward.” I wonder whether imposing a time limit is intended to encourage as much use of ISAs as possible… Another part worth watching is the newly proposed “productive ISA.” The productive ISA comes in two types: general and youth. With a three year contribution period extendable to ten years in total, an annual KRW 20 million limit, and full exemption for interest and dividends (plus a deduction of 10% of contributions for the youth type), it offers far more advantages than the existing ISA. However, investments are limited to “domestic” assets such as Korean stocks, domestic equity funds, and the National Growth Fund. This looks like an attempt to boost the Korean stock market specifically. Since the tax reform proposal was announced, public opinion has been unfavorable because it changes ISA accounts. https://www.khan.co.kr/article/202608072329001 Apparently, the government has ordered a review, perhaps realizing that it does not make sense either. What a relief.

title: Is Naver Blog Dead in 2026?
description: People say Naver Blog is dead, but more people still use it than you might expect.
content: People say Naver Blog is dead, but more people still use it than you might expect. With the arrival of AI, Naver bloggers are losing their place. For most searches, people increasingly prefer ChatGPT over Naver, and even the people writing posts sometimes publish AI generated text exactly as it is. Then what position will Naver Blog move into in the future? Traditionally, Naver search displayed a mix of ads, blog posts, and posts from its online cafés. Because results were shown according to Naver's search rankings, advertising posts were mixed in and credibility suffered. Going forward, I wonder whether Naver's own AI search feature, Naver Mate, will be used to surface more closely relevant information. At some point, my profile started showing how often my posts had been cited. I haven't written many posts, so I wonder where on earth they're being cited. The number was surprisingly high. In other words, AI is evaluating blog posts and deciding which ones to show. The key point is that this isn't a popularity ranking. It sounded to me as though my posts could be cited even if I'm not a power blogger. Nobody is likely to be curious about rambling everyday posts or diary entries like this one. In the end, all we can do is write thoughtfully about things people want to know and hope AI delivers our posts to them well. There are several blogs I've been reading lately, and their authors seem to keep writing without particularly thinking about money. I think doing anything consistently is the hardest part, and in that sense I find those people impressive. People on working holidays in Canada or living abroad seem to start blogs and YouTube channels quite often, perhaps because they have more free time and breathing room. It's good for keeping records and building a habit, so I don't see a downside. In my case, I put them in a group, add them as blog neighbors, and occasionally peek in. I get to see how people in similar circumstances live, sometimes reflect on myself, and find travel destinations, restaurants, and useful tips. Most people try to get information only from particular cafés or online communities, but I think Naver Blog is actually more of a treasure trove and often gets news faster. So my conclusion is: don't think it's too late to start a Naver blog. I'd encourage you to start right now.

title: Game Theory
description: Game theory studies situations in which several people make strategic decisions while anticipating one another’s actions.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ Let’s learn about game theory. Game theory = a theory that studies situations in which several people make strategic decisions while anticipating one another’s actions. For example, whether I lower my prices depends on how a competing company sets its prices. Game theory usually has four basic components: 1\. Player: The decision maker. This may be an individual, a company, a country, and so on. 2\. Strategy: An action available to a player. 3\. Payoff: The result obtained from choosing each strategy. This may be money, profit, utility, a win or loss, and so on. 4\. Information: How much is known about the other player’s actions or circumstances. The most famous example is the prisoner’s dilemma . Two criminals, A and B, each make a choice. B stays silent B betrays A stays silent A 1 / B 1 A 10 / B 0 A betrays A 0 / B 10 A 5 / B 5 If both stay silent, the result is 1, 1, close to the best outcome for them together. But from A’s perspective, betrayal is better whether B stays silent or betrays. The same is true for B. So they may ultimately arrive at A betrays + B betrays = ( 5, 5). In other words, although a better outcome exists for both, pursuing their individual interests leads them to a worse outcome. An important concept here is the dominant strategy . \= A strategy that is advantageous to me regardless of what the other person does. In the prisoner’s dilemma above, betrayal is the dominant strategy. And one of the most important concepts in game theory is Nash equilibrium . \= A state in which changing my strategy alone cannot improve my outcome if everyone else’s strategy stays the same. In the example above, “betray / betray” is the Nash equilibrium. If A alone switches to silence, the result changes from 5 to 10, making A worse off. The same applies to B, so neither has a reason to change strategy alone. A Nash equilibrium does not mean the best outcome for society. Game theory appears incredibly often in real life, including business competition, international relations, and everyday life. Let’s explore game theory through a second example: a zero sum game . As the name suggests, a zero sum game is one in which one side loses exactly what the other gains, so the total payoff is zero. A B Total A wins +10 10 0 Draw 0 0 0 B wins 10 +10 0 The key is that the pie does not grow or shrink. The question is who gets more of an already fixed pie. The other player’s gain is my loss. Most situations involving winners and losers or competition are close to zero sum games. Rock paper scissors is another example. Unlike the prisoner’s dilemma, the more important question in a zero sum game is, “ How much can I take without letting the other person take it from me? ” This introduces the concept of minimax . \= A strategy that minimizes my losses in the worst case scenario. Where the prisoner’s dilemma and rock paper scissors (a zero sum game) are generally games in which choices are made simultaneously, a sequential game is one in which someone acts first and the next person responds after observing that action . The key point is that “who moves first changes strategies and decisions.” Chess is a major example, and this also happens frequently in everyday life. Two new cafés, A and B, are considering opening. A chooses first. A: Should I open a café or not? If A opens, B must decide next. B: Should I open with lower prices, or simply compete? description: Loblaw began in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, in 1919. Theodore Pringle Loblaw, known as T.P. Loblaw, and his business partner J. Milton Cork opened the first Loblaw Groceterias store in Toronto…
content: https://competition bureau.canada.ca/en/how we foster competition/education and outreach/canada needs more grocery competition Loblaws Loblaw began in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, in 1919. Theodore Pringle Loblaw, known as T.P. Loblaw, and his business partner J. Milton Cork opened the first Loblaw Groceterias store in Toronto. Unlike traditional grocery stores, where clerks fetched products for customers, they introduced a self service, cash sales model in which customers selected their own products and paid in cash. Lower operating expenses and the elimination of costs associated with selling on credit allowed them to offer lower prices, and customers responded enthusiastically. Loblaw Groceterias grew rapidly, expanding beyond Ontario into New York State in 1924. By 1928, it had 69 stores and a headquarters and distribution warehouse considered state of the art at the time. When T.P. Loblaw died at age 60 in 1933, the chain had more than 150 stores. The familiar Loblaws name began appearing on store signs in 1939. However, the Weston family, which controls Loblaw today, is not its original founding family. The Westons' business history goes back further, to 1882. Founder George Weston worked in Toronto as an apprentice baker and bread salesman before buying a bread delivery route from his employer and starting his own business. He subsequently grew Weston's Bread into Canada's largest baking business by the early twentieth century. In 1924, his eldest son, Garfield Weston, became president of George Weston Limited. Garfield expanded his father's Toronto bakery into a food company operating across Canada and internationally. He began acquiring Loblaw shares in 1947, buying 100,000 shares, and George Weston Limited secured a controlling interest in Loblaw in the early 1950s. According to the official annual report, George Weston Limited acquired control of Loblaws Inc. in 1953, and the present day Loblaw Companies Limited was established in 1956. Loblaw later struggled with overexpansion and retail competition. A turning point came in the early 1970s when W. Galen Weston , the third generation of the Weston family, became involved in management. After becoming CEO in 1972, he closed unprofitable businesses and refreshed store designs and branding, returning Loblaw to growth. Through this process, Loblaw became a core asset of George Weston Limited and Canada's largest food retailer. Private label brands also played an important role in Loblaw's growth. In 1978, it launched no name , the low price brand famous for its yellow packaging, and opened its first No Frills discount store that same year. In 1984, it introduced President's Choice , emphasizing quality and distinctive products. Today, the two brands serve different roles: no name focuses on low prices, while President's Choice emphasizes quality and new products. Loblaw subsequently built a national network by acquiring regional retailers. It acquired Quebec's Provigo in 1998 and T&T Supermarket, Canada's largest Asian grocery chain, in 2009. Its 2014 acquisition of Shoppers Drug Mart transformed it from a supermarket company into a diversified retailer encompassing food, pharmacies, health, and beauty. The Weston family still effectively controls Loblaw. As of early 2026, Galen G. Weston owns or controls approximately 59.5% of George Weston Limited's shares through companies he controls. George Weston Limited, in turn, holds approximately 52.6% of Loblaw Companies Limited. Galen G. Weston currently chairs the board of Loblaw Companies Limited and serves as both chairman and CEO of its parent, George Weston Limited. Professional executive Per Bank , as president and CEO, is responsible for Loblaw's day to day operations. Separate leaders manage its major business divisions. Frank Gambioli: President of the conventional supermarket division Melanie Singh: President of the discount division, including No Frills and Maxi Tina Lee: CEO of T&T Supermarkets Gregers Wedell Wedellsborg: President of Shoppers Drug Mart In other words, Loblaws and No Frills do not each have their own CEO. Under Loblaw's central leadership, division heads manage conventional supermarkets, discount stores, T&T, Shoppers Drug Mart, and other businesses.
