Sobey. In 1907, he started a meat delivery business using a horse drawn cart in Stellarton, Nova Scotia, Canada. He bought livestock from local farmers, transported it, and resold it. Beginning in 1924, his son, Frank H. Sobey, expanded the business from selling meat and a few vegetables into a full grocery store. In 1947, he opened the first modern Sobeys supermarket in Atlantic Canada, laying the foundation for today's chain. Sobeys Inc. is currently a wholly owned food retail subsidiary of Empire Company Limited. Its major retail banners include Sobeys, Safeway, Thrifty Foods, Foodland, IGA, IGA Extra, FreshCo, Chalo! FreshCo, Lawtons Drugs, and Needs. It also operates the online grocery service Voilà. Empire's food retail division additionally includes Farm Boy, Longo's, and other businesses. James M. Dickson currently chairs Empire Company Limited's board. Pierre St Laurent serves as president and CEO of both Empire Company Limited and Sobeys Inc. He succeeded Michael Medline as CEO, effective immediately, on November 5, 2025. Banners such as Sobeys, Safeway, Foodland, and IGA do not each have a separate CEO. They operate under Empire and Sobeys' integrated leadership. Julia Knox, as Chief Retail Officer and Chief Technology and Innovation Officer, oversees retail operations, the supply chain, and central kitchens. Each region and retail banner has its own operations and store management organization. According to Empire's official disclosures, as of May 2, 2026, its major supermarket banners had 234 Sobeys stores, 132 Safeway stores, 140 IGA Extra stores, 189 IGA stores, 52 Farm Boy stores, 43 Longo's stores, 26 Thrifty Foods stores, and 209 Foodland stores. Quebec banners Bonichoix and Les Marchés Tradition had 45 and 81 locations, respectively. There were also four Kim Phat Asian grocery stores and two Pete's Frootique & Fine Foods specialty grocery stores. The discount supermarket banners FreshCo and Chalo! FreshCo had a combined 160 locations. This total covers both banners: 108 in Ontario, six in Manitoba, five in Saskatchewan, 24 in Alberta, and 17 in British Columbia. Beyond grocery stores, the Sobeys group operates various other retail formats. It had 74 Lawtons Drugs pharmacies, eight Rachelle Béry health and organic specialty stores in Quebec, and 77 Needs convenience stores in Atlantic Canada. Quebec convenience store banners Boni Soir and Voisin had 282 and 80 locations, respectively. The figures also included six Cash & Carry wholesale stores, 359 retail fuel locations, and 97 liquor stores. Voilà is not a conventional physical supermarket banner but an e commerce service handling online orders and delivery. It operates through central customer fulfilment centres, or CFCs, regional delivery hubs, and delivery and pickup networks based at existing stores. Overall, Sobeys has grown from a small meat delivery business in Nova Scotia in 1907 into a national retailer that owns or operates more than 1,600 food retail stores through company ownership, franchises, and affiliates across all ten Canadian provinces. Current Scale As of January 3, 2026, Loblaw operates or manages a total of 2,504 stores in Canada. These include 566 corporate owned stores, 562 franchise stores, and 1,376 Shoppers Drug Mart and Pharmaprix pharmacies operated by independent pharmacists. Including pharmacy clinics and other healthcare facilities, Loblaw describes its total network as more than 2,800 stores, pharmacies, and clinics. Together, its direct employees and franchise and pharmacy personnel number approximately 220,000. About 90% of Canadians live within 10 km of a Loblaw affiliated store. Loblaw's food and pharmacy retail revenue in 2025 was approximately CAD 63.9 billion. Its food, pharmacy, and financial services businesses generate more than one billion customer transactions annually. PC Optimum also has more than 18 million active members. Its history began in Quebec, Canada, in 1947, when independent grocery operators established a joint purchasing organization called Magasins Lasalle Stores. Small grocers struggled to compete on price with large retail chains, so owners joined forces to buy goods together and sell at prices comparable to the major chains. METRO began as an alliance of independent merchants rather than one individual's venture. In 1956, the organization “groupe des épiciers Metro” and the Metro banner were created. In 1972, the company changed its name to Marchés d'Aliments Metro and began operating modern supermarket format stores in earnest. METRO subsequently expanded through mergers with regional grocery distribution organizations. It listed on the Montreal Stock Exchange in 1986. That same year, it acquired pharmaceutical distributor McMahon Distributeur Pharmaceutique, entering pharmacy and pharmaceutical distribution alongside food retail. A series of acquisitions played a major role in making METRO the large retailer it is today. In 1987, it strengthened its discount supermarket business by acquiring Super Carnaval stores. In 1992, it acquired the leases and business rights of 48 stores from Steinberg, then one of Quebec's leading supermarket companies. In 1999, it expanded beyond Quebec by acquiring Loeb and 41 supermarkets in Ontario. One of its most important turning points was the CAD 1.7 billion acquisition of A&P Canada in 2005. This gave METRO a strong retail network in Ontario as well as Quebec, establishing it as a major supermarket company in Canada's two largest food markets. Many of today's Metro and Food Basics stores in Ontario emerged from these acquisitions and subsequent banner reorganizations. Alongside conventional supermarkets and discount stores, METRO continued adding specialty food brands. It acquired a 55% interest in Adonis, a supermarket specializing in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern foods, in 2011, then purchased the remaining interest in 2017. It invested in Quebec bakery brand Première Moisson in 2014 and acquired the founding family's remaining interest in 2019. The 2018 acquisition of pharmacy chain Jean Coutu Group significantly changed METRO's business structure. It transformed METRO from a supermarket company into a diversified retailer spanning food, pharmacies, and health and beauty products. Pharmacy banners including Jean Coutu and Brunet now form the core of METRO's pharmacy business. title: Garbage Collection in Python
description: Examples explaining how reference counting and cyclic garbage collection in Python clean up memory.
content: Garbage collection is the process of cleaning up memory that is no longer used. Let's look at an example. Objects like these, which nothing points to, are called garbage. The process of cleaning up that garbage is garbage collection. Python does most of this automatically. That is why we usually do not free memory ourselves. Python performs garbage collection in two stages. Reference Counting What is reference counting? It means counting how many references point to an object. When the reference count reaches 0, the object is immediately removed from memory. GC GC finds objects that reference counting alone cannot clean up and removes them from memory. A typical example is a cyclic reference . There are no variables through which we can access them, yet their reference counts are not 0. Wrapping Up Python manages garbage collection, or cleaning up unused memory, automatically, so you do not need to manage it yourself. An object that you continue to reference cannot be removed. Cyclic references may be cleaned up later. Resources such as files, connections, and network connections should not be left to GC. References 1. title: Data Structures
description: Data Structures
content: A data structure is a structure for storing and managing data efficiently . The overall classification is as follows. Linear Data Structures Array / List An array is a way of storing multiple ordered pieces of data in a single data structure. Each item has an index, starting at 0. Access by index is very fast: its time complexity is 0(1). Finding a desired value in a list = linear search = brute force In this case, the time required increases as the amount of data grows. String A string is a data type that can be treated like a data structure containing an ordered sequence of characters. You can think of its internal structure as follows. index: 0 1 2 3 4 value: h e l l o That is why you can access it by index, just like a list. Unlike a list, which can be modified, a string cannot be modified. To change a string, you must create a new one. Extracting part of a string = slicing In other words, strings in Python are immutable. Although a string is a data type, you should also be comfortable treating it as a linear data structure. Linked List A data structure in which items are connected to one another by links. A list has an established order. You can access each element's position directly through its index. In a linked list, each item knows where the next item is; it is not a structure that allows direct access through an index. To find a particular value or reach a position, you must follow the links in order from the first node. Insertion or deletion itself is O(1) because only the links need to change, but finding that position usually takes O(n) time. Python does not have a library for using a conventional linked list directly in the same way as a list, so you implement it yourself. Deleting an intermediate node in a makes more sense as removing it from the chain than as deleting it outright. Next, how should we delete the head? Similarly, set head to head.next. Stack A data structure in which the last item to enter is the first to leave, like an elevator. LIFO (Last In, First Out) Items are always added and removed from the top. In Python, you do not use a separate Stack class. The time complexity is O(1). In coding tests, it is often used for parentheses problems, DFS, and undo operations. Queue A data structure in which the first item to enter is the first to leave, like an escalator. FIFO (First In, First Out) In Python, a queue is usually created using rather than . The time complexity is O(1). In coding tests, it is often used for BFS, waiting queues, and problems requiring processing in order. Deque Deque = Double Ended Queue A queue that allows insertion and removal at both ends. All of these have O(1) time complexity. In coding tests, it often appears in BFS, sliding windows, and monotonic queues. Hash based Data Structures Hash Table / Hash Map A hash table is a data structure that stores data as key value pairs. Ultimately, a hash table is a data structure for finding things quickly by key. On average, lookup, insertion, and deletion are close to O(1). title: Looking Back on the First Half of 2026
description: A retrospective template organizing my thoughts and lessons learned on June 30, 2026
content: https://youtu.be/U0TXIXTzJEY Introduction Half of 2026 has passed. On January 1, I wrote a review of 2025 and set goals for the future. At the end of April, when a third of the year had gone by, I wrote another reflection to shake myself out of my laziness. This time, I thought I would write to wrap up the first half of the year. That makes three posts this year that could be called retrospectives. Writing one every quarter might be a good idea going forward. Blogging used to feel burdensome, but these days it feels easier and takes less time. Writing anonymously probably makes a big difference because I can write more freely. Separately, having ChatGPT give my writing a final review has greatly reduced my fear of writing. I started this blog this year. Instead of using a platform such as Naver or Substack, I made a personal blog with a free domain. It is inconvenient. Attaching images to posts is especially tedious, as are categorizing and moving posts. The lack of communication with others is another drawback. I still do not know who reads this blog. Then who am I writing for? I do not really know that either. For now, my purpose is to leave a record. Perhaps that means I am writing for myself. I plan to move over all the posts I previously wrote elsewhere. I do not quite understand why I want to go this far despite the inconvenience. I do not know whether I am doing the right thing, either. A Time of Upheaval Since entering my thirties, I have encountered things I never expected and somehow kept dealing with whatever was in front of me. That is how I ended up living abroad. It had always been a vague possibility, never part of my plan. I need to accept reality, yet there are still many parts I have not accepted. My goal in my twenties was to buy my own home. Naturally, I had been focused solely on buying a home in Korea. I have made more than 130 payments into my housing subscription savings account and saved over KRW 20 million in it. Living abroad makes that dream feel a little farther away for now. Because I keep dealing with what is right in front of me, I do not know what lies beyond it. Sometimes it seems endlessly far away; sometimes it feels like an illusion. The things I cannot handle and keep postponing simply pile up. They are things I will eventually have to resolve, but I avoid them because they are difficult, boring, or bothersome. English, coding, and exercise fall into this category. They take time; you do not suddenly become good at them overnight. Despite knowing better than anyone that consistency brings improvement, I do not do them. Like tidying my desk when exam season approaches, I keep trying to organize my priorities instead. I feel as if I will keep making excuses until everything eventually blows up. Only when it is too late to turn back will I regret it again... This latest cycle brought intense FOMO as semiconductor stocks surged. The only Korean stocks I had held were Samsung, Hyundai Motor, Naver, and entertainment companies. Of course, I sold them all long ago and have not bought any since, so I did not suffer losses. Still, even watching from a distance, I felt enormous envy. It feels as though I have reached a crossroads in life. I keep feeling that I will not be able to live an ordinary life. As polarization worsens, I worry about where I will end up and whether I can endure and keep going. Time to Throw a Stone Into a Calm Lake “Korea is fast and convenient, but uneasy on the mind. Canada is inconvenient and slow, but peaceful on the mind.” I once saw a post like this on Threads, and many people agreed. It was a post I had simply scrolled past, but suddenly I thought it was wrong. When I first came to Canada, the weather was nice and I had no worries. I felt as if I were starting a new life. Perhaps I was conditioning myself to believe, “It is okay; I have only just arrived. Everything will work out later.” And for me to believe that things will improve and that I am happier now, my earlier memories have to be the opposite. Perhaps that is why I decided Korea was an uneasy place and judged Koreans as blunt while liking Canadians because they smiled at me. There are many people in the world, and just as many different kinds of people. Ultimately, whether your mind feels at ease depends on how you think. Anyway, Canada feels as calm as a lake. Of course, considering the cost of living, it is not exactly stable or tranquil. But looking only at the nature and weather, the city certainly has its charm. Now, though, it is time to throw a stone into that lake. I have to survive the ripples that gently spread across it. Only then can I understand how I am staying afloat and whether I am somewhere safe. A jet ski is better than a cheap wooden sailboat, and boarding a yacht or cruise ship would feel safer and more comfortable still. Let me keep assessing where I am and finding ways to upgrade. Review Looking back on the first half of the year, there were no particularly notable achievements apart from a major change in my mindset after visiting Korea in April. I need to reflect on how little diligence I have shown toward my plans. English study is at least one thing I have kept doing, and continuity seems to be what matters. I signed up as a freelancer on Upwork to earn money on the side, but people give me assignments before signing a contract and then never reply. Still, I am trying to think positively: perhaps solving these assignments can help me improve my skills. I should keep better records on the blog so I can review things more thoroughly in my next retrospective. Plans Ahead If it is something I will have to do eventually, let me stop putting it off and get it done quickly. And let me hold firmly to what I planned and push it through to the end so it does not go off course.

title: React State Management
description: Notes on state management in React
content: State = a value that can change over time and that the system needs to remember. React follows the philosophy that "when state changes, the screen changes." Rather than changing the DOM directly, React changes state and recalculates the UI based on that state. useState Because React generally looks at references when checking whether state has changed, you create and assign a new value instead of modifying the existing state directly. This is immutability. React is essentially a tree of components, with parent, child, and sibling relationships. Data flows from top to bottom (parent child). Siblings cannot exchange data directly; it must go through a common parent. Passing data from the bottom up is trickier. Props = values a parent passes down to a child. STATE COLOCATION Keep state as close as possible to where it is used. LIFTING STATE UP When several children need the same state, move it to their nearest common parent. What if the structure gets more complicated? The intermediate components have to keep passing along props they do not actually use. PROPS DRILLING A situation where intermediate components keep passing props down even though they do not use them. Drawbacks 1. Intermediate components need to know about unnecessary information. 2. Changing the structure becomes a hassle. 3. In TypeScript, props types spread unnecessarily. To address these drawbacks, change the component structure or use Context or a global state library such as Zustand, Reducx, or Jotai. CONTEXT API A built in React feature that lets components below access shared values without manually passing props through multiple levels. Context is a feature for passing values. Using Context here lets you skip those intermediate steps. Putting too much information into Context makes it harder to manage later. Use Zustand for more complicated cases. Be careful about putting frequently changing values into Context. Do not put server data in Context. It does not automatically handle caching, refetching, stale time, or updates after mutations. TanStack Query is more appropriate for that case. ZUSTAND Zustand = a library that creates a global store outside React components, allowing components to retrieve only the values they need from that store.

title: Notes on Employment Status and Labour Standards in Canada
description: Notes on employee and contractor differences, wages, overtime, vacation pay, and advisory bodies in Canada and BC
content: This post provides general information as of July 22, 2026, and is not legal advice. Different rules may apply depending on occupation, collective agreements, federally regulated workplaces, averaging agreements, and other circumstances. When working in BC, it is important first to determine whether you are an employee or an independent contractor . Simply having the word contractor in your contract does not settle your status; it may be assessed based on the actual working relationship. The BC Employment Standards Act generally applies to employees and does not apply to independent contractors. Employment status is the most important point. That is because whether protections such as minimum wage, overtime, and vacation pay apply can depend on whether you are an employee or a contractor. Independent contractors generally handle their own taxes and CPP. EI does not apply automatically in the same way as it does for employees, and EI special benefits for self employed people have separate registration requirements and conditions. When joining as an employee: Offer Letter + Employment Agreement. When working as a contractor: Independent Contractor Agreement / Service Agreement. For employees, basic protections do not disappear simply because the role is called full time, part time, temporary, or permanent. However, there are exceptions for managers and certain occupations. The second point is wage information. Minimum wage = the minimum hourly wage. It varies by province. Pay period = the period used to calculate wages. In BC, wages must generally be paid at least twice a month, and a pay period cannot exceed 16 days. Paystub = wages before tax. Tips = gratuities. Final pay = the timing of the final wage payment after resignation or dismissal. Record keeping = working hours. Under BC's general rules, overtime pay applies to work exceeding eight hours a day or 40 hours a week . Daily overtime (over eight hours a day) / Weekly overtime (over 40 hours a week). Double time (over 12 hours a day). Split shift (when a day's work is divided into separate shifts). Meal break (time for meals/rest). The same applies to part time and full time employees. Next, you should know about vacation pay and holiday pay. In BC, after five days of employment, vacation pay generally accrues at a minimum of 4% of total wages. After five consecutive years of employment, the minimum is 6%. Pay Matters In Canada/BC, salary negotiations themselves are not a company's legal obligation. There is no law requiring a company to hold an annual salary negotiation or raise salaries by the rate of inflation. However, an adjustment may become mandatory when the minimum wage rises, an increase is promised in the employment contract, a role changes with a new pay agreement, or company policies require it. Put simply, salary increases are more a matter of negotiation and market rates than law. They are a negotiation, not a right. Conversely, a significant unilateral change to wages or working hours may raise an issue of constructive dismissal, depending on the contract and the facts. Because this requires an individual assessment, it is safer to check with the Employment Standards Branch or an employment lawyer. title: Python HTTP Client Libraries
description: Notes on the concepts behind Python HTTP client libraries
content: The Python HTTP client libraries we will look at today do not really have much to do with coding tests. However, if you later work as a web developer, you may often need them for external API calls, crawling, communication between servers, and authentication requests. I am currently studying Python as a backend language, and because these are widely used, foundational Python libraries, I decided to write down the basics to get a general understanding. Some representative libraries are , , , , , , , and . Let's start with the fundamentals: HTTP and HTTPS. What is HTTP? HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol It is a set of communication rules that allows clients and servers to exchange data. On the web, a browser uses HTTP to request pages or data from a server. In other words, HTTP is the way clients and servers talk to each other on the web. What is HTTPS? HTTPS = HTTP Secure It basically exchanges requests and responses in the same way as HTTP, but adds an encryption layer called TLS. HTTP + TLS With HTTP alone, someone in the middle may be able to snoop on the data. HTTPS, on the other hand, encrypts communication between the client and server, allowing sensitive data such as login credentials and payment information to be exchanged more securely. Most websites today use HTTPS. What is TLS? TLS = Transport Layer Security A security technology that protects data exchanged between clients and servers over the internet by encrypting it. TLS provides: 1. Encryption: Makes the content difficult to read even if someone intercepts it. 2. Authentication: Checks that the server you have connected to really is the intended server. 3. Integrity: Checks that the data has not been tampered with along the way. A simplified version of the process looks like this: The browser requests a connection to the server The server sends a TLS certificate The browser verifies the certificate Both sides securely agree on keys to use for encryption They then exchange encrypted HTTP data. This process is called a TLS handshake.

title: International Schools
description: An overview of international schools
content: The original purpose of international schools was quite practical. They were created so that children of diplomats, expatriate employees, staff of foreign companies, missionaries, and families who moved frequently between countries could continue their education wherever they went. Over time, they came to be seen as a route to a global elite education. In particular, parents usually send their children to international schools for the following reasons. 1. An English speaking environment 2. Admission to universities abroad 3. Avoiding Korea's competitive entrance exam system 4. Networking 5. An approach to education centered on discussion, presentations, and research 6. Giving their children a wider range of choices There may be many reasons, but there is no doubt that the fundamental motivation starts with wanting one's own child to do even a little better. International schools are categorized according to which country's curriculum they follow. Entry ages and graduation structures vary somewhat by curriculum, but they usually have a K–12 system extending from kindergarten through high school graduation. The subjects, assessment methods, teaching methods, and approach to university preparation differ from those of ordinary Korean schools. Typical curricula include: American: American Curriculum, AP, SAT/ACT British: British Curriculum, IGCSE, A Level IB: PYP, MYP, DP Canadian: Ontario, BC, Alberta Curriculum, and others Australian: Australian Curriculum European: French, German, Swiss, and others Hybrid: American + IB, British + IB Korean: Korea's national curriculum, school grades, and the CSAT In other words, the curriculum you choose also changes the direction of university admissions. Among these, the IB is relatively versatile and widely used for admission to universities in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Europe, and Asia. There are generally four characteristics of an international school. First, it follows an overseas curriculum. Second, most classes are taught in English or another foreign language. Third, it has international or curriculum accreditation from organizations such as WASC, CIS, NEASC, IB, or Cambridge International. Fourth, it has a system for transcripts, recommendations, counseling, and essay guidance for admission to universities abroad. In one sentence, an international school should be "a school that operates an overseas curriculum primarily in English, with international accreditation and a system for admission to universities abroad." In Korea, the terms international school, foreign school, foreign educational institution, and alternative school are used interchangeably, making them easy to confuse. There are often said to be seven "authorized international schools that Korean nationals can enter without a history of living abroad": Chadwick International, Daegu International School, Calvin Manitoba International School, NLCS Jeju, Branksome Hall Asia, St. Johnsbury Academy Jeju, and KIS Jeju High School. Foreign schools, on the other hand, are different in nature. Well known foreign schools such as Seoul Foreign School, Seoul International School, and Yongsan International School are schools operating with education office authorization, rather than academies outside the formal system. However, because their original purpose is to educate foreign children, Korean nationals often face additional admission requirements, such as a history of residence abroad. Diplomas also need to be distinguished. Graduating from a foreign or international school may provide a school diploma, a High School Diploma, an IB Diploma, or A Level results. However, this does not automatically mean recognition as a high school graduate in the Republic of Korea. Domestic academic recognition can depend on the school's authorization category, its designation for academic recognition, and completion of Korean language and social studies/Korean history courses. Particular care is needed with unauthorized international schools or alternative English language schools. Even if a school has "International School" in its name, its qualifications may not be recognized domestically. In that case, only middle school or an earlier level of education may be recognized in Korea, and a qualification examination may be needed for admission to a Korean university. When choosing a school, therefore, be sure to check domestic academic recognition, the type of diploma, overseas university admission results, and international accreditation. While Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States were popular destinations for international schools in the past, Malaysia, Singapore, India, and Dubai are attracting considerable attention these days. Why Do English Speaking Countries Need International Schools? In Korea, one of the biggest reasons for choosing an international school is an "English speaking environment." But in countries such as Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia, where English is already an official language, international schools mean something a little different. There, they are less about simply learning English and more about admitting international students, offering an international curriculum such as the IB, or providing boarding facilities. Seen this way, international schools in Korea are, in some respects, used for purposes somewhat different from their original intent. They were originally created to maintain continuity in education for the children of diplomats, expatriate employees, foreign company staff, and families with frequent international moves. In Korea, however, English education, overseas university admission, avoidance of the Korean entrance exam system, social mobility, and networks have become strongly attached to that purpose. Of course, being an English speaking country does not mean there is no educational competition. Private tutoring, prestigious private schools, and a strong emphasis on education certainly exist in British Columbia, Canada, too. However, rather than "international schools" functioning as a major separate category as they do in Korea, the structure is closer to public school international student programs, private/independent schools, IB schools, and boarding schools. The following are often mentioned among BC's well known private schools: St. George’s School Crofton House School York House School West Point Grey Academy Collingwood School Mulgrave School Stratford Hall Brookes Westshore Bodwell High School Pearson College UWC In other words, international schools in English speaking countries are less "schools for learning English" and more schools with international curricula, international students, boarding, and university admission systems. That makes me wonder whether immigrating or studying abroad at a young age is, in practice, much like attending an international school, since students use English and follow that country's curriculum. Tuition Tuition at international schools and private schools abroad generally starts in the KRW 30 million range per year. Admission fees, uniforms, textbooks, activity fees, donations, and transportation may be added. Including boarding, you should budget around KRW 50 million to KRW 100 million per year. Add vacation programs and university consulting, and an enormous amount of money is needed. Sending a child to an international school means committing a tremendous amount of funding. It is not easy. Checklist Before Choosing an International School [ ] School authorization category [ ] Domestic academic recognition [ ] Curriculum [ ] Type of diploma [ ] University admission results [ ] Teaching staff [ ] Student nationality mix [ ] Tuition [ ] Transfer options [ ] English support programs [ ] Quality of counselors

title: Understanding Duck Typing in Python
description: An explanation of duck typing in Python and how it differs from isinstance(), with examples
content: Duck typing is a way of working with objects based on whether they have the methods or attributes you need, rather than their actual class. In Python, code is often written around calling the required operation and seeing whether it can be used, instead of first checking for a particular type. Duck typing is a term you encounter when learning about objects and classes in Python. Its name is said to come from the old expression, "If it walks like a duck, and quacks like a duck, it is a duck." In programming, this means placing more importance on whether an object has the functionality you need than on the class it was created from. If it has the required functionality, you can use it as though it were that type. Although well known in Python, this way of thinking is common across dynamically typed languages. Let's look at an example. First, we have classes for a dog and a cat. In the code above, make sound() does not check whether an object is a Dog, Cat, or Robot. Instead, it only looks at whether the sound() method can be used. Dog, Cat, and Robot are different classes, but they can all be used in the same function because each has a sound() method. When you first encounter duck typing, you might think, "Isn't this just using a method if it exists? Isn't that obvious?" In fact, if you only use Python, the concept may not feel particularly special or important. But that "seemingly obvious approach" is exactly what duck typing is about. Duck typing does not first check whether an object belongs to a particular class, as isinstance(obj, Duck) does. Instead, it works with objects by checking whether the functionality you need can actually be used, as with obj.quack(). In other words, rather than asking, "Is this object an instance of the Duck class?", you ask, "Can this object quack()?" This approach is one of Python's natural characteristics. isinstance() is a function that checks whether an object was created from a particular class/type. Duck typing is an important way of thinking that lets Python code work flexibly. However, a missing method causes an error at runtime, so it is a good idea to make the expected behavior clear through function names and exception handling.

title: Notes on the Canadian School System

content: In Canada, education falls under provincial rather than federal jurisdiction. School systems and registration procedures therefore vary somewhat between BC, Ontario, and Alberta. Public school placement is generally based on a student's residential address. The area of addresses assigned to a particular school is called a school catchment or catchment area. Each region has a school district or school board that manages its schools, and student registration follows that authority's procedures. Living within a catchment area can give you priority for enrollment at that school, but admission is not always guaranteed, depending on capacity and registration timing. If you want to send your child to a good school district, there are only three options: 1. Move into the catchment area. 2. Submit a cross boundary / cross district application. 3. Apply through a special program. In BC, I would say with confidence that West Vancouver is an area with good schools. For one thing, it has high housing prices and a high cost of living. It is similar to Seoul's Gangnam School District 8, although the atmosphere is quite different. You might wonder, "How does that make it a good school district?" People here do not place as much emphasis on school districts, but if you were to compare them, the public schools themselves have a good reputation. It is said that roughly 97–98% of students graduate each year, and over 87% of graduates go on to a post secondary institution. title: Thoughts on AI
description: Thoughts on the possibilities of AI as a tool and the need to guard against overconfidence
content: I feel as though I have become someone who finds it difficult to do anything without AI. Turn that statement around, though, and it also means that with AI, I feel I could try anything. Of course, I probably cannot fully match someone with advanced skills. But given time, I think I could at least imitate their methods to some extent. That is why I believe overconfidence is the attitude we must be most careful about when using AI. AI is becoming an extension of the smartphone. In the past, producing something meaningful on the internet meant sitting at a desk and spending a long time on it. Now, even without a laptop, we can code remotely using just a smartphone, and the results are much better than before. AI helps me do what I am good at even better, and enables me to do things I cannot do on my own. In some ways, it feels all purpose. But while it can find efficient answers to choice based questions such as “Should I do A or B?”, it does not first tell me what I truly want. For now, AI remains something we use. It is a tool that appears when we need empathy, calculations, or help and fulfills our requirements. But people must ultimately decide what they want, where to go, and which problems to solve. That is why sound or creative thinking is necessary. With the arrival of AI, the cost of production is moving closer and closer to zero. In the future, as data repeatedly becomes more distributed and scattered or consolidates into just one or two surviving super apps, the gap will grow wider.

content: This post provides general information as of July 22, 2026, and is not personalized tax or investment advice. Limits and eligibility may change from year to year or depending on individual circumstances, so check your CRA account and consult a tax professional before filing or contributing. In Canada, individuals generally file an income tax return each year. Filing and payment deadlines vary depending on personal circumstances, self employment status, and other factors, so it is safest to check the CRA's tax filing deadlines first. Rather than assuming it is "always suitable for short term investing," you should choose an account based on your goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance. Maximizing contributions to an FHSA or RRSP is not necessarily the best choice for everyone either. Emergency funds, debt costs, current and expected retirement tax rates, and home buying plans should all be considered together. Do not assume you qualify just from the name; check the CRA's eligibility guidance. Self employed people can generally deduct reasonable current expenses incurred to earn income, but cannot deduct personal expenses. For costs that combine personal and business use, separate out only the business portion and retain supporting records such as receipts, contracts, and usage logs. title: Python Basics
description: Notes on Python syntax and basic concepts
content: Variables Unlike JavaScript, there are no keywords such as let, const, or var. You simply write the variable name. Conditional Statements Instead of {}, indentation separates code blocks. Comparison Operators : equal to : not equal to : less than : greater than : less than or equal to : greater than or equal to : logical AND : logical OR : logical NOT Loops (for, while) For loops are commonly used in Python and can iterate over various data structures, including lists, dictionaries, and sets. You can also use while loops, but for loops are more concise and easier to read. There is no do...while loop. break, continue : terminates the loop immediately. : skips the current iteration and moves to the next one. Functions Functions are defined with the keyword. A function can accept input values, or arguments, through parameters, perform a particular task, and return a result. Lists Lists are defined with square brackets and can contain various data types. Lists are mutable, so you can add, remove, and modify their elements. There are various list methods, including append, insert, remove, pop, clear, sort, and reverse. You can create lists concisely using list comprehensions. Dictionaries Dictionaries are defined with curly braces and store data as key value pairs. Dictionaries are mutable, so you can add, remove, and modify their elements. Dictionary methods include keys, values, items, get, and pop. Working with Strings Strings can be defined with single quotes or double quotes . Strings are immutable and can be manipulated through various methods. Reading and Writing Files Use the function to read and write files. You must specify a mode when opening a file: typically for reading, for writing, and for appending. Exception Handling Exceptions are handled using and blocks. Put code that may raise an exception in the block, and the code to run when an exception occurs in the block. Common Exception Types | Exception | Meaning | | | | | ValueError | Invalid value | | TypeError | Incorrect type | | IndexError | List index out of range | | KeyError | Accessing a missing dictionary key | | ZeroDivisionError | Division by zero | | FileNotFoundError | File does not exist | There is also else. There is also finally. It always runs, whether the operation succeeds or fails. raise lets you trigger an error yourself. Importing Other Functionality (import / module) In Python, each .py file is a module, and import is used to bring its functions, variables, classes, and other contents into another file. For example: Here, calculator.py is a module. Here, import calculator imports the module from the calculator.py file. Not just functions, but variables are part of modules too. Functions, variables, and classes written in a file basically become attributes of the module. Unlike JS/TS, Python has no export keyword. Frequently Used Python Standard Library Modules 1. math (a module for mathematical calculations) 2. random (used to generate random values) Keep in mind that random does not provide randomness for security purposes. For security related values such as passwords, tokens, and verification codes, secrets is more appropriate. 3. datetime (used to work with dates and times) 4. os 5. sys 6. pathlib 7. json 8. collections 9. itertools 10. heapq 11. bisect 12. re 13. ... Working with File Paths (pathlib) A library that works with file paths as Path objects rather than strings. When writing a program that reads or saves files, it is used to specify reliably exactly where the file being handled is located. For example: reading CSV files, reading JSON configuration files, saving image files, creating log files, saving scraped data, organizing uploaded files, loading documents for AI/RAG, and creating backups. Relative and absolute paths Relative path: a path relative to the current working directory. Absolute path: the complete path starting from the computer's root. JSON How to save Python dict / list data to a file, or read a JSON file back into Python data. CSV Used to work with tabular data. package / pip / virtual environments / uv External libraries, excluding built in libraries such as json, pathlib, and math, are called packages. package = a collection of Python functionality created by others, or a library. requests = HTTP requests fastapi = backend API server pandas = data analysis numpy = numerical computation python dotenv = reading .env environment variables pytest = testing pip is a tool for installing Python packages, like npm install in Node.js. Virtual environments were introduced to configure package versions independently for each directory or server. venv = a Python environment dedicated to a project. When someone else receives your project, they do not know which packages to install. That is why the installation list is written in a file called requirements.txt. requirements.txt manages only the package list. A project has more to manage than its package list: its name, version, Python version, dependencies, test settings, linter settings, formatter settings, build settings, and so on. title: One-Third of 2026 Has Passed
description: It feels as though we were saying “Happy New Year” just the other day. I can’t believe it’s already May.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, source: OGQ It feels as though we were saying "Happy New Year" just the other day. I can't believe it's already May. From January through March, I more or less muddled along. Actually, I had a trip to Korea planned for April, and the anticipation kept me going. Going back to Korea was the biggest event for me. I spent the month of April there. Visiting Korea brought up feelings I'd never experienced while living there. I don't know whether I've written this before, but I dislike the phrase "the smarter you are, the sooner you leave Korea." No matter how severe the divisions between genders and generations or the political crises, Korea is still undoubtedly a good country to live in. I probably wouldn't have realized that if I'd continued living there. And strangely, some Koreans living in Canada seem to hate Korea intensely. I can't understand it, and if I can avoid people like that, I'd like to. One thing that always comes up when discussing Korea is its culture of constantly comparing people. In the past, I probably would have thought that tendency was unhealthy too, but now I wonder whether it's really bad—as long as you're not putting others down through those comparisons. While working in Korea, I may not have noticed because I was surrounded by that culture. Of course, it was stressful, and pursuing a higher salary meant I felt compelled to live an intensely disciplined, productive life. At the same time, I came to think that living diligently isn't necessarily a bad thing. I think unfairness would be a more reasonable reason to dislike Korea than comparison itself. In online communities, I sometimes see demoralizing comments like "They're kicking away the ladder upward" or "No more dragons will rise from humble streams." But there are circumstances we cannot choose from birth, so everyone inevitably starts somewhere different. I think we have to accept that to some extent, and beyond that, I still feel there are opportunities. Perhaps living abroad is what helped me realize this, too. I reflect on how shameful it was to speak badly of my own country. Especially now, when its standing is rising, I shouldn't go against that. Separately, I should become more active on the blog, if only to leave a record. It's a promise I fail to keep every time, but... I'm making the commitment again.

title: Looking into SH’s Mirinaejip Housing Program

content: https://www.i sh.co.kr/main/lay2/S1T7312C7332/contents.do I learned about a rental housing program called “Mirinaejip” run by SH (Seoul Housing & Communities Corporation). The apartment type includes major branded apartment complexes, which has attracted a lot of attention. Naturally, applicants must not own a home. title: Taking HarvardX CS50x Online in the Age of AI
description: “Will developers really disappear in the age of AI?” “If so, what should I do with my life?”
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ “Will developers really disappear in the age of AI?” “If so, what should I do with my life?” These are among the thoughts I return to most often these days. As AI keeps advancing, it is replacing more and more human work. Of course, this is not unique to AI. It has happened repeatedly throughout the history of industrial development. The difference now is that the scope and scale of what AI replaces are much greater. As time passes, much of the work humans have traditionally done will eventually be replaced. That also means AI will be able to take over even areas based on the abilities we have considered uniquely human, such as our five senses. So we now need to think about something beyond those senses. Lately, I have been calling this “the realm we need to transcend into”: invisible things such as inspiration and intuition, often called a sixth sense, or what people commonly call “taste.” I also use AI a great deal at work. It has clearly increased my productivity and enabled me to do things I could not do before. My learning curve feels much steeper, too. On the other hand, there are times when I am not sure whether the results I achieve this way are truly mine. That is why I think I must be even more careful not to become conceited. That is a principle I hold for myself. With so called vibe coding, you can put something together almost instantly. It is easy to feel pleased with yourself when you see the result. I watch out for that feeling, too. We are receiving help from AI right now, but we cannot be sure that help will always be available as a matter of course. For example, if ChatGPT or Claude goes down, we run out of tokens, or costs keep rising, we could find ourselves in a difficult situation. I think we need to prepare for those possibilities as well. That is why I started taking Harvard University’s CS50 course. I expect fewer students to enroll in university in the future and more schools to close. The population is declining, degrees matter less than they used to, and there are fewer and fewer reasons why education must happen in person. Even so, some things never change. I call them “the essentials.” The essence of being a developer is not simply writing code to build something. Ultimately, a developer is someone who solves problems in a structured way. Of course, AI makes identifying and solving problems much faster. But the more I use it, the more I sometimes find myself feeling helpless in proportion to my reliance on it. That is another reason I do not want to depend on AI excessively. So I plan to finish the course and strengthen my computational thinking, even a little. To develop a more flexible and creative way of thinking.

title: Wins & Opps
description: I happened to come across the phrase “wins & opps” while reading a fellow blogger’s post.
content: © Vera Lúcia, Source: OGQ I happened to come across the phrase “wins & opps” while reading a fellow blogger’s post. It was my first time hearing it, so I asked ChatGPT. Apparently, it is shorthand for things that went well (or achievements) and areas for improvement. Put simply, it is a performance report. I am not sure whether my current company will negotiate my salary or simply notify me of an increase, but it seems to be talent review season. The blogger said they had completed a Talent Review. It varies by company and role, but the categories were as follows. What you did MSO and Job Description What you did Business Goalds How you did it Competencies How you can grow Ongoing Development How you can grow Career Aspirations I remember doing something similar in Korea, but perhaps I have become less alert to these things and settled into this life. It has already been almost a year since I joined the company. I think I have done a lot during that time, but results are what ultimately matter. I should think through the categories above to evaluate myself. There might be an unexpected opportunity to negotiate my salary… And it would also help me prepare early for a job change. I really want to change jobs this year.

title: Thoughts I’ve Been Having Lately
description: The phrase “every person for themselves” lodged itself in my mind.
content: © yassine amsloh, source: OGQ Just a year ago, the phrase "every person for themselves" lodged itself in my mind. It was when the first digit of my age changed from two to three. Looking back now, I was reckless and immature then. It was also a time when I lacked a sense of responsibility. The same is true even now. Comparing myself today with who I was a year ago, not much has changed. But I've experienced so much, and ahead of me lie only things that will bring more responsibility. I feel a tangle of emotions that are hard to explain, but if I were to put it in one sentence, I think it would be: "My main job comes first." At least once in life, everyone faces a moment so difficult that they feel like letting go of life itself. If it's something I have to do anyway, pain is only natural. If I can get it over with, it's better to do so quickly.

title: Suncor Energy Company Analysis
description: A brief analysis of Suncor Energy's business structure, revenue model, growth drivers, and risks
content: The following is a brief overview of the Canadian company Suncor Energy (ticker: SU, NYSE/TSX). 1. Company Overview Founded: 1919 as a Canadian affiliate of Sun Company; rebranded as Suncor in 1979 Headquarters: Calgary, Alberta Core business: Integrated energy, including oil sands development, refining, and oil and gas exploration and production Major assets: Alberta oil sands reserves, three refineries in Edmonton, Chicago, and Ontario, and wind generation assets on the east and west coasts Official website: https://www.suncor.com/ Suncor Energy is Canada's largest integrated energy company, spanning the value chain from bitumen extraction in the oil sands to refining, oil and gas exploration and production, and renewable energy investment. Its strategy integrates upstream oil sands operations with downstream refining to create synergies across the value chain. 1.1. Investment Characteristics Energy stock characteristics (35%): Upstream earnings directly linked to crude oil prices Infrastructure characteristics (25%): Stable cash generation from long term assets, including refineries and oil sands facilities Growth stock characteristics (15%): Growth through expanding oil sands production and improving refining margins Dividend stock characteristics (10%): A consistent dividend policy supported by stable cash flow Cyclical characteristics (10%): Sensitive to global energy demand and economic activity Thematic characteristics (5%): Exposure to investment in the energy transition and carbon neutrality 1.2. Core Business Model Suncor's core competitive strength lies in optimizing the value chain through upstream downstream integration: Upstream : Oil sands bitumen extraction and initial processing, including operation of the City upgrader Midstream : Pipelines and storage facilities, through owned assets and equity investments Downstream : Refining and the production and marketing of petrochemical products at refineries in Edmonton, Chicago, and Ontario Renewable energy : Wind power projects and low carbon technology investment, through internal development and partnerships This integrated model cushions crude oil price fluctuations. Downstream operations lead earnings when refining margins are strong, while upstream operations lead when crude prices are high. 2. Background and Management Background: Began in 1919 as a Canadian affiliate of Sun Company and played a pioneering role in oil sands development. Following its 1979 rebranding as Suncor, it continued pursuing an integration strategy. Management focus: Prefers strategies emphasizing operating efficiency, capital discipline, and long term value creation. CEO: Rich Kruger 3. Products and Revenue Structure Oil sands upstream: Bitumen extraction and upgrading, approximately 40% of revenue Refining and petrochemicals: Production and sale of petroleum products such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, approximately 35% of revenue Exploration and production (E&P): Development and production of conventional oil and gas deposits, approximately 15% of revenue Renewable energy and other: Wind generated electricity sales and low carbon solutions, approximately 10% of revenue Earnings primarily depend on hydrocarbon sales volumes and prices. Upstream profitability centers on per barrel costs, while downstream profitability is determined by refining margins, or crack spreads. Its distinctive earnings structure combines the long term nature of oil sands operations with the cyclical nature of refining. 4. Market and Competitive Environment The distinctive nature of oil sands development creates high barriers to entry in Canada's energy market. Competition among established players centers on production cost efficiency, reserve scale, and the degree of value chain integration. Major competitors include integrated energy companies and specialized upstream producers. 4.1. Similar Companies and Competitors Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ): A balanced portfolio of oil sands and conventional oil and gas Imperial Oil (IMO): An ExxonMobil affiliate with strengths in refining Cenovus Energy (CVE): An oil sands producer pursuing integration through its recent acquisition of Husky MEG Energy (MEG): Specializes in steam assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) oil sands extraction Birchcliff Energy (BIR): Specializes in conventional natural gas and liquefied natural gas 5. Growth Drivers Improved oil sands production efficiency and advances in technology that lowers operating costs Better downstream profitability from stronger refining margins Low carbon investment and commercialization of carbon capture and storage (CCS) Refinery efficiency improvements and product slate optimization Expansion of renewable energy assets and growth in electricity sales Stronger global competitiveness through access to U.S. Gulf Coast refining markets 6. Key Risks Direct exposure to crude oil price fluctuations, including reliance on Brent and WTI prices Higher operating costs from tighter carbon regulations and rising carbon taxes Environmental controversy around oil sands and unfavorable perceptions within ESG investing Construction delays and cost overruns on major projects Scheduled refinery maintenance and unexpected shutdowns Changes in Alberta's energy and tax policies Possible oversupply in U.S. Midwest refining markets, linked to rising Permian Basin production 7. Points to Watch Daily oil sands production and per barrel operating costs Refinery utilization and margins in Canadian and U.S. Midwest markets Trends in upstream and downstream operating margins Capital spending and free cash flow generation Debt ratios and interest coverage Progress in reducing carbon intensity and the scale of low carbon investment Progress on renewable energy projects and electricity sales contracts Conclusion As a pioneer in Canadian oil sands development and an integrated energy company, Suncor Energy has a distinctive business model built on upstream downstream value chain integration. Although exposed to crude oil price cycles, its ability to moderate earnings volatility through integration and its long term oil sands assets form the foundation for medium and long term value creation. Amid environmental regulatory pressure and the energy transition, it is adapting through operating improvements, low carbon technology investment, and expansion of its renewable energy portfolio. These efforts will be central to maintaining its competitiveness as a Canadian energy company.

title: Wheaton Precious Metals Company Analysis
description: A brief analysis of Wheaton Precious Metals' business structure, revenue model, growth drivers, and risks
content: The following is a brief overview of the Canadian company Wheaton Precious Metals (ticker: WPM, NYSE/TSX). 1. Company Overview Founded: 2004 as Silver Wheaton; rebranded as Wheaton Precious Metals in 2017 Headquarters: Vancouver, British Columbia Core business: Precious metals streaming and royalties, including silver, gold, and palladium Major assets: A portfolio of streaming contracts with mine operators around the world Official website: https://www.wheatonpm.com/ Wheaton Precious Metals is the world's largest precious metals streaming company. It provides upfront payments during mine development and operations in exchange for the right to purchase future silver, gold, and other production at predetermined low prices. Rather than owning mines itself, it relies on contracts with mining partners. Through this business model involving non income producing assets, it offers leveraged exposure to rising precious metals prices. 1.1. Investment Characteristics Precious metals price exposure (40%): Earnings directly linked to silver and gold prices through streaming margins Royalty characteristics (25%): Stable cash generation based on long term contracts Growth stock characteristics (15%): Growth through new streaming agreements and portfolio expansion Dividend stock characteristics (10%): A consistent dividend policy supported by stable cash flow Infrastructure characteristics (5%): Long term, contract based asset characteristics Defensive characteristics (5%): Increasing demand for precious metals as safe havens during financial crises 1.2. Core Business Model Wheaton's core competitive strength lies in optimizing precious metals price exposure through streaming contracts: Upfront payment : Providing cash during mine development or expansion, usually 10–20% of the total expected purchase amount Streaming purchase rights : Securing the right to buy a fixed share of future production at a predetermined low price Silver: Usually 5–25% of production at a fixed price of approximately $4–6 per ounce Gold: Usually 3–15% of production at a fixed price of approximately $400–600 per ounce Immediate sale or holding : Selling purchased metals immediately at market prices or holding them to realize additional gains if prices rise Under this model, mining partners bear operating risks such as extraction difficulties and permitting issues, while Wheaton takes leveraged exposure to rising precious metals prices. Its cash costs are very low compared with conventional mining companies, and margin volatility is limited. 2. Background and Management Background: Began in 2004 as Silver Wheaton, specializing in silver streaming, then expanded into gold streaming. Its 2017 rebranding as Wheaton Precious Metals accompanied diversification into palladium and other precious metals. Management focus: Prefers strategies emphasizing contract design, partner relationships, and efficient capital allocation. CEO: Randy Smallwood 3. Products and Revenue Structure Silver streaming: Contracts with silver producing mines worldwide, approximately 60% of revenue Gold streaming: Contracts with gold producing mines worldwide, approximately 30% of revenue Other precious metals: Streaming contracts for palladium, platinum, and others, approximately 10% of revenue Earnings primarily come from selling metals obtained through streaming at market prices. Streaming margins—the difference between market prices and streaming purchase prices—are central to profitability. Because it has no mining costs of its own, its cash cost structure is highly favorable compared with conventional miners, and it has significant operating leverage when precious metals prices rise. 4. Market and Competitive Environment The precious metals streaming and royalty market is oligopolistic because it requires specialized expertise and relies on long term contracts. Competition among major players centers on contract quality, including purchase price, scale, and duration, and the creditworthiness of partners. New entrants need substantial capital and long term partner networks. 4.1. Similar Companies and Competitors Franco Nevada (FNV): Strong in gold streaming and royalties, with a diversified resource portfolio Royal Gold (RGLD): Primarily royalty focused, diversified across gold, copper, and other resources Osisko Gold Royalties (OR): Combines gold streaming and royalties with its own mine development Sandstorm Gold (SAND): A young growth company specializing in gold streaming Maverix Metals (MMX): A diversified metals streaming portfolio 5. Growth Drivers Portfolio expansion through new streaming agreements, particularly with development stage mines Increased production and extension negotiations under existing contracts Wider margins in a rising silver and gold price environment Diversification into palladium and other precious metals Innovations in streaming structures, including perpetual streams and interest rate linked structures Benefits from production growth at major mining partners 6. Key Risks Direct exposure to declining precious metals prices, particularly silver and gold Operational problems at major mining partners, including extraction difficulties, permitting issues, and labor disputes Deteriorating partner creditworthiness and risks to contract performance Difficulty finding new deals and worsening contract terms as competition increases Structural downside pressure from lower industrial silver demand, including solar power and electronics Greater appeal of alternative investments as interest rates rise, which disadvantages non income producing precious metals Major contracts expiring and potentially unfavorable renegotiation terms 7. Points to Watch Silver and gold production secured through streaming, measured in ounces Streaming margin levels and trends, including purchase prices relative to market prices Average remaining duration of the contract portfolio Size and terms of new contracts, including upfront payments, streaming percentages, and purchase prices Cash flow generation and dividends relative to free cash flow Debt structure and interest burden Production guidance and earnings trends at major mining partners Share price movements relative to silver and gold, including beta and correlation Conclusion As the world's largest precious metals streaming company, Wheaton Precious Metals has a distinctive business model involving non income producing assets that offers leveraged exposure to rising precious metals prices without taking on mine operating risks. Its highly favorable cash cost structure and substantial operating leverage relative to conventional miners tend to support strong performance in precious metals bull markets. Although exposed to metal price fluctuations, stable cash generation from long term contracts and risk management through portfolio diversification underpin medium and long term value creation. In particular, its balanced exposure to silver, with substantial industrial demand, and gold as a safe haven asset may provide stability across different market conditions.

title: Brookfield Asset Management Company Analysis
description: A brief analysis of Brookfield Asset Management's business structure, revenue model, growth drivers, and risks
content: The following is a brief overview of the Canadian company Brookfield Asset Management (ticker: BAM, NYSE/TSX). 1. Company Overview Founded: 1899 as Brookfield's predecessor; reorganized into a holding company structure under Brookfield Corporation (BN) in 2021 Headquarters: Toronto, Ontario Core business: Alternative asset management on behalf of pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and insurers Major locations: Financial hubs across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific Official website: https://www.brookfield.com/ Brookfield Asset Management manages alternative investments on behalf of institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and insurers, earning management and performance fees. Unlike the holding company BN, its business model focuses on fees generated from third party capital. 1.1. Investment Characteristics Fee based earnings (40%): Stable management fees and variable incentive fees Growth stock characteristics (25%): Growth through expanding alternative investment AUM and new fundraising Cyclical characteristics (15%): Earnings vary with fundraising conditions and investment returns Dividend stock characteristics (5%): A lower payout ratio than BN, with most earnings reinvested Thematic characteristics (10%): Exposure to expanding alternative investment, infrastructure, and the energy transition Defensive characteristics (5%): Some earnings stability from long term contracts 1.2. The Essential BN vs. BAM Structure Brookfield reorganized into a holding company structure in 2021, separating BN, the holding company, and BAM, the asset manager: BAM, the asset manager : Manages third party capital, including pension funds, earning management fees BN, the holding company : Invests its own capital directly, focusing on dividends and asset appreciation AUM scale and fundraising ability are BAM's central sources of value creation. 2. Background and Management Background: Started as a Canadian business in 1899, built its position in infrastructure and real estate investment throughout the twentieth century, and specialized in alternative asset management in the 2000s. Management strengths: Using global networks, designing complex alternative investment structures, and investing for the long term. CEO: Sachin Shah, the CEO responsible for BAM, a separate role within the Brookfield group 3. Products and Revenue Structure Alternative investment funds: Diversified strategies spanning infrastructure, private equity (PE), real estate, renewable energy, and credit Revenue structure: Management fees: Annual fees of approximately 1.0–1.5% of AUM, a stable revenue source Incentive fees: Additional fees when returns exceed a specified hurdle rate, a variable revenue source Dividend income: Dividends from affiliates such as BN, representing a small share Investment strategy: Applying active operating capabilities and sector expertise to create long term value Approximately 80–90% of revenue comes from management fees, providing a relatively stable earnings structure. Performance fees offer additional upside. 4. Market and Competitive Environment High barriers to entry make alternative asset management an oligopolistic market. Its major competitors are large global managers, while the market is expanding with growing demand for alternative investments. New entrants need brand credibility, an investment track record, and a global network. Competition among established firms centers on attracting AUM and delivering performance. 4.1. Similar Companies and Competitors Blackstone (BX): The world's largest alternative asset manager, focused on real estate, private equity, and credit KKR (KKR): Expanding from private equity into infrastructure and credit Carlyle (CG): Global manager combining private equity and credit Apollo (APO): Alternative investment platform with significant credit and insurance asset management exposure TPG (TPG): Specializes in private equity and growth capital EQT (EQT): Northern Europe based manager specializing in growth capital 5. Growth Drivers Greater alternative investment allocations by pension and sovereign wealth funds, driven by the need to diversify returns in low rate environments Broader access to alternatives for individual investors through innovative fund structures and platforms Increasing long term investment demand for infrastructure and the energy transition Restructuring and specialization in private equity markets Continued growth in global pension assets and higher target allocations to alternatives 6. Key Risks Stagnant AUM growth if fundraising conditions deteriorate Lower performance fees and weaker reinvestment incentives when returns disappoint Fee pressure from increasing competition in alternative investments Difficulty attracting and retaining key talent, given reliance on star managers Regulatory changes and greater disclosure requirements, particularly in private equity Indirect effects from changes in the asset values of affiliates such as BN 7. Points to Watch AUM size and growth, including quarterly trends Fundraising pace and new fund closings Trends in management fee rates Performance fee shares and average returns, including the proportion above hurdle rates Changes in allocation across strategies such as infrastructure, PE, and real estate Major investment track records and earnings announcements Conclusion Brookfield Asset Management is a leading global alternative asset manager. Its fee focused business model, based on third party capital, supports stable earnings generation. Although it has some economic exposure, structural growth in demand for alternatives and its global network provide medium and long term growth drivers. Investment performance creates volatility, but the management fee based earnings structure may help limit downside risk.

title: Canadian Pacific Kansas City Company Analysis
description: A brief analysis of Canadian Pacific Kansas City's business structure, revenue model, growth drivers, and risks
content: The following is a brief overview of the Canadian company Canadian Pacific Kansas City (ticker: CP, NYSE/TSX). 1. Company Overview Founded: 2021 through the merger of Canadian Pacific and Kansas City Southern, whose histories date to 1881 and 1887, respectively Headquarters: Calgary, Alberta Core business: Operating a transcontinental North American rail freight network connecting Canada, the central and southern United States, and Mexico Major assets: Approximately 32,000 km of rail lines connecting Western Canada with the U.S. Midwest and South and Mexico Official website: https://www.cpr.ca/ Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CP) operates the first and only single railway network connecting Western Canada, the U.S. Midwest and South, and Mexico. It provides integrated logistics solutions for grain, energy products, intermodal freight, automobiles, and consumer goods. Access to South American markets through Mexico is a distinctive competitive strength. 1.1. Investment Characteristics Infrastructure characteristics (30%): Stable cash flow based on an exclusive route network Cyclical characteristics (25%): Directly linked to industrial production and trade volumes, particularly automobiles and industrial goods Dividend stock characteristics (15%): Consistent dividend growth supported by stable cash flow Value stock characteristics (15%): Can be valued based on assets and cash generating ability Growth stock characteristics (10%): Margin expansion through operating improvements and price increases Thematic characteristics (5%): Exposure to intra North American trade, supply chain restructuring, and access to South American markets through Mexico 1.2. Core Business Structure Freight transportation: Transporting diverse categories, including intermodal freight, raw materials, and consumer goods Network efficiency: Optimizing on time delivery, fuel efficiency, and asset utilization Additional services: Logistics solutions, warehousing, supply chain management, and single carrier service 2. Background and Management Background: Established in 2021 through the merger of Canadian Pacific (CP) and Kansas City Southern (K), whose histories date to 1881 and 1887, respectively. The merger completed a single carrier network connecting Western Canada with Mexico. Management focus: Prefers strategies emphasizing operating efficiency, safety management, and customer service quality. CEO: Keith Creel 3. Products and Revenue Structure Intermodal transportation: Containers and trailers, approximately 45% of revenue Commodity transportation: Grain, fertilizer, petroleum, and chemicals, approximately 30% of revenue Consumer and industrial goods: Finished products, automotive parts, paper products, and more, approximately 25% of revenue Revenue primarily consists of freight charges based on volume and distance. Network optimization and asset utilization are central to profitability. A particular strength is that single carrier service can reduce transfer costs and time. 4. Market and Competitive Environment High barriers to entry make the North American railway industry an oligopoly. Canadian National Railway (CNI) and Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CP) form the main Canadian duopoly, while partially competing with Class I railways in the United States.
