title: Brookfield Corporation Company Analysis
description: A brief analysis of Brookfield Corporation's business structure, revenue model, growth drivers, and risks
content: The following is a brief overview of the Canadian company Brookfield Corporation (ticker: BN, NYSE/TSX). 1. Company Overview Founded: 1899 Headquarters: Toronto, Ontario Core businesses: Alternative asset management and investment in real assets, including infrastructure, renewable energy, real estate, and private equity Official website: https://www.brookfield.com/ Major locations: Financial hubs across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific Organizational structure: A holding company with decentralized business operations Brookfield Corporation is a global alternative asset manager and owner of real assets. Its core earnings sources are long term management fees and investment returns from asset appreciation. 1.1. The Two Main Pillars: BN vs. BAM Brookfield Corporation (BN): Acts as the holding company, investing its own capital for the long term and focusing on dividends and asset appreciation Capital sources: Its own equity and cash flow from owned assets Earnings sources: Dividends and distributions from assets, plus asset appreciation Character: Compound growth through long term ownership and reinvestment Brookfield Asset Management (BAM): Acts as the asset manager, investing on behalf of pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and insurers, with a focus on fee revenue Capital sources: Third party institutional capital Earnings sources: Management fees, which are stable, and performance fees, which are variable Character: AUM growth and fundraising capability are central 1.2. Investment Characteristics Blue chip characteristics (30%): Stable cash flows from long term real assets and a global portfolio Growth stock characteristics (20%): Aims for compound growth through alternative investment AUM expansion and capital reinvestment Value stock characteristics (10%): May be viewed as a value stock by investors who consider it undervalued relative to its assets Dividend stock characteristics (10%): Pays dividends, but the core focus is long term compound growth and reinvestment Defensive characteristics (10%): Some defensive cash flows, though economic and interest rate conditions can cause fluctuations Thematic characteristics (15%): Exposure to long term themes such as infrastructure, the energy transition, and data centers REIT status (0%): A holding company style alternative asset manager, not a REIT; it owns real estate and infrastructure but does not have a REIT structure Commodity exposure (5%): Not directly a commodity company, but its portfolio may have indirect exposure 2. Background and Management Background: Began as a Canadian asset based business and expanded into a global alternative investment group focused on infrastructure and real estate. Management strengths: Long term capital allocation, infrastructure operations, and management of complex asset portfolios. CEO: Bruce Flatt 3. Products and Revenue Structure Asset management: Management and performance fees from alternative investment funds Real asset investment: Cash flows from infrastructure, renewable energy, real estate, and private equity assets Investment structure: A compound growth strategy focused on long term ownership and reinvestment Earnings combine the stability of management fees with cash flow generated by real assets. 3.1. Capital Recycling: The Key to Sustaining ROE Capital recycling is one of Brookfield's core competitive strengths. Rather than simply holding assets, it improves their value, sells portions to recover capital, and reinvests in growth assets. Asset acquisition: Secure real assets that are undervalued or have room for improvement Value enhancement: Improve operating efficiency, contract structures, and scale Partial sales: Realize gains by selling stakes in mature assets Capital recovery: Redeploy recovered capital into new investments Reinvestment: Focus allocation on assets in their growth phase This structure increases capital turnover and helps explain why ROE can remain high over long periods. Compared with Blackstone, Brookfield also has a stronger identity centered on operating real assets and repeating this recycling process. 4. Market and Competitive Environment Competitors include global alternative asset managers such as Blackstone, Apollo, and KKR, as well as the direct investment capabilities of major pension and sovereign wealth funds. Brookfield seeks to differentiate itself through its real asset operating capabilities and global network. 4.1. Similar Companies and Competitors Blackstone (BX): Global alternative asset manager focused on real estate, private equity, and credit Apollo (APO): Alternative investment platform with a large share of credit and insurance asset management KKR (KKR): Expanding from private equity into infrastructure and credit Carlyle (CG): Global manager combining private equity and credit Ares Management (ARES): Asset manager focused on credit and alternative lending 4.2. BN vs. BAM: Which Is Better for Shareholders? One of investors' most common questions is whether BN or BAM is more attractive. Since the two have clearly different characteristics, the answer depends on the investment objective. BN, the holding company: Asset appreciation and compound growth, with relatively greater volatility BAM, the asset manager: Fee based stability and predictability, with growth dependent on AUM expansion In essence, BN is a bet on asset value and long term compound growth, while BAM suits investors who prefer the stability of fee based cash flows. 5. Growth Drivers Rising power and infrastructure demand and greater investment in the energy transition Higher alternative investment allocations by pension funds and institutional investors Long term global demand for real assets such as data centers, logistics, and power grids Stable capital allocation through a diversified asset portfolio 6. Key Risks Higher capital costs from rising interest rates Asset value fluctuations and liquidity risks Increasing competition in alternative investments Regulation and approval delays for infrastructure projects 6.1. Brookfield and the Interest Rate Cycle Interest rates are an important variable for Brookfield, but rising rates cannot simply be treated as unqualified bad news. Fixed vs. floating rates: The impact depends on the debt structure; a higher fixed rate share provides more protection Inflation linked contracts: Many infrastructure contracts are linked to inflation, helping protect cash flow in an inflationary environment Long term contracts: Long term agreements and regulated earnings cushion the impact of rate changes In other words, even when rates rise, the actual effect can vary with the asset mix and contract structure. 7. Points to Watch Growth in assets under management (AUM) and fundraising progress Cash flow stability in infrastructure and renewable energy assets Results from capital recycling: selling assets and reinvesting the proceeds Debt structure and management of interest rate sensitivity Conclusion Brookfield Corporation has a distinctive structure combining alternative asset management with ownership of real assets, focusing on long term compound growth. It may be sensitive to interest rates and asset values, but global demand for infrastructure and the energy transition provides medium and long term growth drivers.

title: Credit Card Recommendations in Canada

content: Introduction Affiliate disclosure: This post includes the author's American Express referral link. If a card is approved through that link, the author may receive a points reward. You may have kept using the card you first got, without experiencing much inconvenience, wondering whether you really need to get another one, and finding it a hassle to research which card to apply for. Even so, I strongly recommend spending a little time learning about credit cards and making use of them. In these times of high prices, shouldn't we at least make efforts like this to spend a little more wisely? Why Is the Amex Cobalt Good? The card people in Canada use most is the Amex Cobalt. Amex, or American Express, has a premium image among Koreans, so many assume its approval requirements are strict, but that is not the case. In fact, its credit limits can be more generous than those of regular banks, so getting the card may be helpful when settling in or planning a large expense. title: Which AI Tools Should I Use?
description: Perhaps because vibe coding has become so popular, even non-developers can now code easily. Sometimes they build things better than developers do. That may be why so many people seem to be starting their own projects or websites as a side hustle.
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, Source: OGQ Perhaps because vibe coding has become so popular, even non developers can now code easily. Sometimes they build things better than developers do. That may be why so many people seem to be starting their own projects or websites as a side hustle. For some, it is a hobby, and things may vary by industry. But at least for people whose jobs involve using a computer, an AI subscription has become a necessity rather than an option. Since this is the age of AI, I also tried to replace everything with AI platforms so I could keep up. My usual combination was ChatGPT + Cursor + Comet + Figma, with only ChatGPT on a paid subscription. After reading that the Comet browser was not secure, I stopped using it. When I heard that Cursor's Solidity extension had security vulnerabilities, I immediately went back to VSCode, too. Fortunately, I could use the features available in Cursor in VSCode as well. The trouble was that the free credit allowance was far too small. Maybe I had already become too used to working with AI. I could not resist and paid for Copilot. I am quite happy with it. As many people had predicted, I could really feel the equation taking shape: money = credits = access to powerful AI tools = time saved. Once this equation has been fully proven, I thought, it might become difficult to use AI as cheaply as we do now. Reality feels like a game. AI companies encourage us to spend, and in games, it is hard to beat paying players. Unless you are aiming to become a top ranked player, it is best to get the most enjoyment from a reasonable amount of spending. So let me compare and organize the AI tools to get as much value as possible. Fortunately, there are not that many AI companies, so there was not too much to agonize over. OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude Code, Github Copilot, Meta MetaAI(Llama), \ Coming soon xAI Glok, Deepseek Microsoft VSCode Google Antigravity Cursor Perplexity Comet OpenAI Atlas Google NotebookLM Midjourney Figma These may be all we need to keep an eye on. For now, at least. Whenever a company announces a new model, people benchmark it and compare its performance. Honestly, keeping up every time is exhausting. Let us put aside who will win and first find the tools that suit us. New AI companies are appearing, but my conservative nature makes me cheer for the established players, Microsoft and Google, rather than readily embrace something new. I think that is a bad habit. https://medium.com/hashed kr/vibe founders 64f178fe5497 While writing this, I came across an article by Simon Seojoon Kim, CEO of HASHED. Once again, I feel that AI really is the paradigm of our time. And an opportunity has arrived in front of us. The era of succeeding on thoughts and ideas alone is over. From now on, it is about execution and persistence.

title: Routine Is Everything
description: After years of setting annual goals, I’m now writing about the importance of a consistent routine.
content: Every New Year, I've set goals for the year ahead. In 2019: Establish my values The people around me In 2020: Health: keep up with the gym, swimming, and looking after my body Volunteer work Reading: 30 books Be good to my parents Dating Unfortunately, I have no record for 2021. In 2022, I wrote a bucket list of things I wanted to do in my twenties. Get waxed Take a family portrait Resign/change jobs 100 million won Travel abroad or travel alone Stay at a five star hotel Join a club In 2023, the goals seem to have evolved into something more specific. Personal development goals Read 10 books Earn one certification: Computer Specialist in Spreadsheet & Database, Level 1 Complete my public speaking classes Move up a level at my English academy Finish all the Udemy courses I've bought: Rust, Golang, TypeScript, Git... Reach 1,000 Twitter followers Habits Exercise at least once a week Consistently do forward head posture stretches every morning Arrive at work early: one hour before the scheduled time Wash up within an hour of getting home Clean up immediately after eating Reduce unnecessary time on social media: TikTok, Instagram, YouTube Finance I'd like to create one source of side income Other If I change jobs, don't let the break between them exceed one month In 2024, I wrote a reflection in Notion, looking back on my twenties and what I'd done well and poorly. I think that was when I began writing reflections rather than New Year's plans. My annual goals seem to be almost the same each year, and I achieve about half while failing at the rest. So now I tend to use the New Year simply to reset my mindset rather than make another set of goals. I recently posted my reflection on 2025 on the blog. At the end, I briefly mentioned my plans for this year, 2026. Nothing grand—just taking care of my health. This year's goals won't be much different from before: I plan to focus on routine. Ever since I saw the phrase, " If you keep doing it, it will become familiar; once it's familiar, you'll naturally get good at it, " I've come to believe that " routine is everything. " Separately, I think the biggest event will probably be preparing for our wedding.

title: 2025: A Year in Review
description: Everyone has been writing year-end reflections, so I thought I’d try one too… It’s been a very long time.
content: Everyone has been writing year end reflections, so I thought I'd try one too. It's been a very long time since I wrote something like this. 1. Life Lately To start with an update: as some of you know, I'm living in Canada now. It's already been nine months since my girlfriend and I came here. As always, I'm doing well. In 2025, I spent more time overseas—two months in the Philippines and nine in Canada—than in Korea. Everything was new and unfamiliar. Living with an uncertain immigration status made me anxious, but being exposed to new things and feeling a daily rush of dopamine may be why time passed especially quickly. It was a year full of varied experiences and plenty of opportunities to think. Honestly, comparing life here with life in Korea, I'm not sure which is better. Looking at Korea from outside, I've come to feel that there are few places as good to live in. But perhaps because I have fewer people to compare myself with, I feel much more at ease mentally. Personally, I like it here, but I also find myself worrying. I'm now thirty in international age. I still don't know whether interrupting the career I'd built in Korea to come to Canada and do something new was the right choice. What is certain is that this was a period when I made a major decision in my life. 2. Concerns If you've only seen me on social media, my seemingly carefree life may look happy against the backdrop of Korea's unstable political situation. I simply don't express it much; inside, I live with a great many worries. My career in blockchain ended in June 2024 and has remained on hold ever since. It's been quite a while since I wrote under the nickname I'd used for years, "Yona." In my mind, Yona is already dead. No—I killed that identity myself. Actually, I lost money in the Luna collapse, and perhaps it had already died then. Looking back again, I feel incredibly lucky that someone like me, who had simply been a crypto obsessive, got to enter and work in this industry. Back then, I enjoyed everything about looking into blockchain, and before AI became as widely used as it is now, I thought blockchain was the future. I used to enjoy browsing overseas Twitter accounts and forums, but now I can just ask ChatGPT to translate or summarize everything, and some of the interest has faded. I'm grateful to live in such an amazing world, but I also have plenty to worry about. I think I've been more anxious and concerned about the future than ever before. Even so, I'm trying to stay as positive as possible and feel grateful to the many people around me. 3. Looking Back I've always gone through life feeling that I'm very ordinary and very lucky. After coming to Canada, I reviewed my résumé. Looking over everything from the part time jobs I'd had as a university student to my last company, I felt proud that I'd worked hard. Maybe that's also why I've adapted well here in Canada. In particular, I first entered the blockchain industry thanks to Twitter (X), and I think Facebook helped me join my second company. I don't think my writing was especially good, so I'm deeply grateful that people saw it positively. I'm also very sorry that I may not have met their expectations or delivered the performance I should have, considering the time I spent there. As an aside, I don't particularly like social media. But it has brought me many opportunities and benefits, so I wonder whether I should make more effort with it going forward. I think entering this industry as a researcher was a really good choice. It taught me the pleasure of activities that satisfy intellectual curiosity. If I'd realized that a little sooner, I might have done better at school, which leaves me with some regret. 4. Relationships I have so much fun spending time with my girlfriend. She is my lifelong partner and also my fiancée. Because of that, I feel like I've forgotten what relationships outside of her even are. Honestly, perhaps I don't really feel the need for them. In 2026, I should at least practice reaching out first to ask the people around me how they're doing. 5. Plans for the Future Health. It may be a clichéd New Year's goal, but lately I really feel the need to take care of it. In my twenties, my parents would greet me on the phone by asking whether I'd eaten. Since I entered my thirties, they've started urging me to go out and exercise as well. More than anything, health seems to matter most. I hope everyone around me stays healthy. For me, 2025 marked the beginning of my thirties. When I wrote last year's reflection and looked back on my twenties, I wished, "I hope I keep being a lucky person." Perhaps that's why I was so lucky. I received an enormous amount of help from people around me after coming to Canada. Following my plans and going with the flow, I lived reasonably well. I can't rely on this luck forever, so I hope 2026 will be a year of growth in many different ways. I wanted to write a clear, well organized reflection like other people, but after finishing it, I realized it wasn't as easy as I'd expected. Still, I'm leaving this record so I can look back on it in 2027.

title: On the Brink of an Era of Upheaval
description: Ten years ago, security specialists ranked among the most promising careers. Five years ago, remote-friendly developer jobs became hugely popular during COVID-19. Even a year ago, AI wasn’t the talking point it is today; ChatGPT’s writing, images, and code still seemed to lack something…
content: © CoolPubilcDomains, source: OGQ Ten years ago, security specialists ranked among the most promising careers. Just five years ago, developer jobs that allowed remote work became hugely popular during the COVID era. Even a year ago, AI—artificial intelligence—wasn't the talking point it is today. I think that was because the writing, images, and source code ChatGPT produced always seemed to lack something. As time passes, AI's capabilities are growing at an astonishing rate. Now I've reached the point where I actually trust AI tools and struggle without them. As everyone knows, the AI era is coming. Or perhaps it has already arrived. As industries advance and paradigms shift, some jobs disappear and new ones emerge. In other words, this is a signal that someone may be facing a golden opportunity. I often wonder, "What jobs can't AI replace?" and "What can only humans do?" I believe that even jobs requiring people to physically use their bodies, such as plumbers, electricians, and hairdressers, could eventually be replaced by machines. After all, every invention so far has come into being to make human tasks—especially repetitive ones—more convenient. That's why I feel thinking is the most important thing. People say AI can think for itself, but ultimately all it does is read and learn from data quickly. (At least, that seems to be the case for now.) It looks as though it creates something new, but much of it is similar to what already exists. In the end, thinking is a uniquely human act. We should strive to be people who think creatively. If technology ever gave us the superpower to read someone's thoughts, as we've seen in films, I feel society would truly become lifeless. AI is a form of computing, and what computers do best is repetition. They can work 24 hours a day without becoming tired, burning out, or getting bored. Humans, on the other hand, can't do that, so we inevitably fall behind. Faced with this, we can't help feeling both helplessness and loss. I don't know what significance writing like this will have in the future. It might serve only as personal note taking. This post, too, was written to organize and record my thoughts.

title: Sorting Through My Weekend Thoughts
description: The weekend went by so quickly that I can barely remember what I did. Weekends always seem to be like that. They always feel short.
content: The weekend went by so quickly that I can barely remember what I did. Weekends always seem to be like that. They always feel short. title: Read This Before Studying for CELPIP
description: I would confidently say that people studying for CELPIP are aiming to obtain permanent residence in Canada. I think I recently saw that Australia also accepts CELPIP scores for immigration, but that is a very recent policy, and for now it is mainly Canadian permanent-residence applicants taking the test…
content: English is essential. I would confidently say that people studying for CELPIP are aiming to obtain permanent residence in Canada. I think I recently saw that Australia also accepts CELPIP scores during immigration assessment, but that is a very recent policy, and for now it is mainly people applying for Canadian permanent residence who take the test. Some people also need English scores for academic purposes, such as university, graduate school, or college admission, but they seem to mainly take IELTS Academic or the Duolingo test. For permanent residence, Duolingo is not yet accepted, and CELPIP is easier than IELTS General, costs less, and provides results faster , so people tend to prefer CELPIP. In fact, that is the whole reason to study for CELPIP. CELPIP = A test for Canadian immigration We need to remember that we are taking this test because we need an English score, not to become good at English. Of course, everyone has a different study style, but if the goal is a high score, we should focus our preparation on that and finish once we achieve it. Canada’s Express Entry permanent residence program is points based, so a higher English score puts you in a better position. First, we need to understand CELPIP properly. (This post is a personal set of notes using the official CELPIP website and ChatGPT to gain a deeper understanding of CELPIP. Please note that it is not a post sharing or recommending study methods.) 1\. Official CELPIP website https://www.celpip.ca/ Home CELPIP \ The test costs $290 + tax. \ The sections are taken in the order L R W S. \ Total time is about two hours and 50 minutes. \ After registering for an account, you can take two practice tests. It seems useful to sign up, assess your current level, and familiarize yourself with the overall test first. Additional paid practice test sets are also sold separately. 2\. Official CELPIP YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/@CELPIPOfficial/videos CELPIP Test The channel uploads videos analyzing the task types in each section and explaining how to prepare. They might be good to listen to on the commute to and from work. 3\. Task types by section Part Task type Questions / Time Content Listening (38 questions total / Approximately 47–55 minutes) Part 1 Problme Solving 8 questions / 11–13 minutes A conversation between two people solving an everyday problem (reservations, schedules, purchases, breakdowns). Select the necessary information. Part 2 Daily Life Conversation 5 questions Everyday conversation among friends, family, or colleagues. Identify feelings, intentions, and details. Part 3 Listening for Information 6 questions One person explains a place, rules, or a procedure. Information matching questions. Part 4 News Item 5 questions Listen to a news item and identify key facts, numbers, and the sequence of events. Part 5 Discussion 8 questions Several people discuss a topic. Distinguish their different opinions and arguments. Part 6 Viewpoints 6 questions One person gives an extended opinion. Identify attitude, feelings, and supporting reasons. Reading (38 questions total / 55–60 minutes) Part 1 Correspondence 11 questions / 9–13 minutes Read an email or message and identify the sender’s intentions, feelings, and the content of a response. Part 2 Apply a Diagram 8 questions / 9–13 minutes Use a notice, table, or diagram to find the option that meets the conditions. Part 3 Reading for Information 9 questions / 10–15 minutes A longer informational text, such as a notice or explanation. Identify facts and details. Part 4 Reading for Viewpoints 10 questions / 13–18 minutes An opinion or argument piece. Questions about the writer’s attitude, supporting reasons, and comparisons. Writing (2 tasks total / 53 minutes) Part 1 Writing an Email 1 task / 27 minutes Write an email with a clear purpose: explain a situation, make a request, suggest a solution, and so on. Part 2 Responding to Survey Questions 1 task / 26 minutes Choose one of two options → Give at least three reasons with specific explanations. Speaking (8 tasks total / Approximately 15–20 minutes) Part 1 Giving Advice 30 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond A friend has a concern → Offer two or three pieces of advice. Part 2 Personal Experience 30 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Describe an actual personal experience naturally. Part 3 Describing a Scene 30 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Describe what is visible in a photo or picture, focusing on people, actions, and the situation. Part 4 Making Predictions 30 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Look at a scene and predict what will happen next. Part 5 Comparing & Persuading 60 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Compare two options → Persuade the other person. Part 6 Difficult Situation 60 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Propose a solution to an awkward situation. Polite requests and explanations are important. Part 7 Expressing Opinions 30 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Give an opinion on a topic with two or three reasons. Part 8 Unusual Situation 30 seconds to prepare / 90 seconds to respond Describe an “unusual situation” (for example, a strange scene). Creativity is needed. 4\. CELPIP Score Comparison Chart https://www.celpip.ca/prepare for celpip/score comparison chart 2/ Score Comparison Chart CELPIP This test does not assign different point values to different questions. In other words, you just need to get as many questions right as possible. Minimize mistakes and make sure to get every question you can answer right. Since the test lasts almost three hours, concentration is essential. If you have taken a recognized English test such as IELTS, TOEIC, or TOEFL before, this probably will not feel much different. If you have to take CELPIP anyway, I hope you prepare well and get the score you need in one attempt. In terms of money and time, simply spending a long time on this test does not necessarily improve your result, and it does not seem worth that much prolonged effort.

title: A Complete Guide to a Working Holiday in Vancouver, Canada: Location, Flights, eSIM, Insurance, Temporary Accommodation, Documents, and Packing
description: I am currently in Canada on a working holiday.
content: ※ This post was brought over from my previous blog during a move. (Originally written: April 12, 2025) I am currently in Canada on a working holiday. I decided to go on a working holiday because I had wanted to become good at English for a long time. Before coming, I completed two months of English language study in the Philippines. Now I have to put it into practice in Canada... There was a lot to prepare to get here, and I thought it would be useful to keep a record on my blog, so I am writing this post. 1. Working Holiday — Canada A working holiday gives you a work visa rather than a tourist visa, allowing you to stay for about one to two years. You can work, learn English, travel, and pursue various other goals. Popular destinations include Japan, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. From 2024, Canada raised its age limit from 30 to 35 and changed the permitted stay to two years. I chose Canada because it is an immigrant friendly, English speaking country. Application requirements and procedures differ by country, so I recommend checking them yourself. – (a) Apply for a working holiday through IRCC – (b) Wait to receive an invitation – (c) Medical examination – (d) Biometrics – (e) Submit the various documents The process can be broken down this way. It seems that final selection can take as little as a month. I remember the cost being approximately KRW 200,000–300,000. https://cafe.naver.com/gocan 2026 Canada Working Holiday No.1...: Naver Cafe The Naver Canada Working Holiday community has detailed instructions, so I recommend joining and following them step by step. Even someone who is not good at English should be able to do it easily. 2. Choosing a Location — Vancouver Canada is a federal country made up of ten provinces and three territories. Its capital is Ottawa, Ontario. The most popular choices for working holiday participants seem to be \ \ Toronto, Vancouver, and Calgary\ \ . Some also go to Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Quebec also uses French, so adapting there may take more effort than in other regions. A brief introduction to each region: – Toronto: Urban, with plenty of jobs and cultural activities; housing and living costs are relatively high. – Vancouver: City and nature; housing and living costs are relatively high; it rains a lot. – Calgary: Nature; living costs are relatively low compared with other regions because Alberta does not charge provincial sales tax (PST). Each province will have more characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages. I recommend choosing based on the environment you want. 3. Flights — March, With a Connection Flights are usually cheapest around three months before departure. Flights connecting through Hong Kong or Japan will probably be the cheapest. Before arriving in Canada, I stopped in Hong Kong for a day of sightseeing, which I really enjoyed. I flew with Hong Kong Airlines. Reviews often mentioned fairly frequent cancellations and delays and strict baggage rules, but it was inexpensive and my trip went smoothly. 4. Mobile Service (eSIM) — Supercell eSIM, Fido Most people suspend their Korean mobile service or switch to a budget plan before leaving. Because I might occasionally need to receive verification messages from Korea, I switched to a KRW 3,300 per month plan that lets me receive texts and decided to use an eSIM. https://blog.naver.com/supercell33 Supercell in Canada! Canadian SIM Cards and Internet Specialists: Naver Blog The most convenient option is to activate an eSIM through a company called Supercell while still in Korea. I received a free 500 MB eSIM coupon when booking accommodation in Hong Kong, so I had planned to sign up locally after arriving in Canada. But the promotions turned out to be the same, and I was not comfortable with English... In the end, I used Supercell to activate my eSIM after arriving. They kindly answered all my questions and seemed to provide consultations late into the night, too... Canada's major carriers are Rogers Bell Telus, with budget brands Fido Virgin Plus Koodo. People say Canadian internet speeds are disappointing compared with Korea. Normally I would have insisted on the leading carrier... But Koodo had the best promotion when I signed up, so I chose Koodo. Promotions seem to change often, so I recommend consulting them before signing up. 5. Travel Insurance — MyBank There were not many insurers offering two year travel insurance in the first place. I heard that signing up through links provided by the community offered a discount, so I chose MyBank, which was said to be the cheapest. I often saw posts saying coverage had to be $50,000 and the term had to be two years. To avoid problems at entry, I chose the “Deundeun” plan, I think, for peace of mind. 6. Temporary Accommodation — Airbnb Unless you are enrolling in a language school, people commonly book Korean run accommodation or a homestay through a Vancouver Korean community, or book an Airbnb. Personally, I recommend Airbnb. There have recently been many room rental scams, and an Airbnb booking lets you print proof of temporary accommodation later. I needed this document when getting my visa and SIN. If you are looking for long term rather than temporary accommodation, focus on neighborhood safety. 7. Essential Documents — International Driving Permit, Travel Insurance Copy, Work Permit Copy, Temporary Accommodation, and Proof of Funds If you want to get a driver's licence in Vancouver, bring an international driving permit and an English language driver's licence (get a new one issued and submit the previous one). At airport immigration, they only checked my work permit and temporary accommodation address. 8. Other Things to Pack... A card that allows overseas cash withdrawals, such as Travel SOL or Travel Wallet I did not buy extra baggage. I brought a 23 kg checked bag, a 7 kg carry on, and a backpack. YouTube and other blogs recommended bringing plenty of clothes, towels, and especially socks, so I packed as much as I could. I looked at some socks at Walmart the other day, and the quality really was poor... I am not sure whether an electric heating mat is essential, but rooms are very dry... The hair dryer I brought is too weak because the voltage does not match. It seems better to buy electronics here where possible. I recommend buying them through departure sales in working holiday communities. 9. Things to Do After Arriving in Canada – Install essential Canadian apps – Get a SIN – Open a Canadian bank account. Banks also have promotions, so check carefully before opening one. I hear customer numbers rank RBC CIBC TD. Make an appointment before going. – Buy a transit card, the Compass Card – Exchange your identification for a BCID – Get a Vancouver Public Library (VPL) card – Sign up for MSP after three months – Find a job I had put together a lot of notes while preparing for my working holiday, so I wrote this based on them. If anything is missing or you have questions, please leave a comment. Thank you 🙂

title: Hiring Is Like a Blind Date
description: It has been almost six months since I stopped working. Looking back on that time, I have rested well and learned a great deal through various experiences. Of course, I am still learning. Since graduating from high school, going to university, serving in the military, and finding work…
content: ※ This post was moved from my previous blog during a migration. (Originally written: November 13, 2024) It has been almost six months since I stopped working. Looking back on what I have done, I have rested well and learned a great deal through various experiences. Of course, I am still learning. Across the years since high school graduation, university, military service, and employment, I have never had a break this long. I think I was lucky. Perhaps I was able to keep moving from one stage to the next because I was constantly prepared. From a career perspective, taking time off is a career interruption. That is why it can be seen as a blemish on a résumé or something to fear. I do not consider this period a loss at all, and I doubt I will regret it later. The biggest change during this break has been in how I think. Today, it suddenly occurred to me that the hiring process is very much like a blind date. You have probably heard that “an interview is also an opportunity for you to choose the company,” or that “an interview is like a blind date.” In fact, I have only been on one blind date in my life, but luckily, I met my current girlfriend on that first date. My experience is limited, but having tried it, I recommend going on blind dates or dating if you have the opportunity. It is unfortunate when young people do not get to date or experience relationships. A blind date usually has a matchmaker. Job platforms such as Saramin and LinkedIn play that role in hiring. A blind date may start with someone asking, “Would you like to meet so and so?” The job market is not quite that kind. Still, there are similarities. Being asked that question by a matchmaker generally happens in two situations: when you are trying to date but things are not working out, or when you have stirred someone’s sympathy. Similarly, if you want a job, it is important to let people around you know you are looking. That is why I see activities such as blogging and using LinkedIn positively. If you do nothing, nothing happens. You have probably seen people around you who go on blind dates often. Why is that? Why has no one ever asked you, “Would you like to go on a blind date?” If you know the answer, that is good; if you do not, take a moment to reflect. Most problems come down to you, and often to a lack of preparation. The same applies in the job market. If you were prepared to be the person companies wanted, you would have many more employment opportunities. Fortunately, I think hiring is somewhat easier than blind dating. Before meeting someone on a blind date, you have no idea what they like or how they think. In hiring, on the other hand, companies tell you in their job postings what kind of person and what skills they need, so there is much more information you can use to prepare. Just as there are lines that tend to work and qualities people seek on a blind date, companies have their own preferred candidates and requirements. So instead of seeing a posting and mindlessly submitting your résumé with a click, take a close look at whether the company suits you, tailor your résumé, and then apply. That is also a matter of basic courtesy. An interview is the first meeting with the other party. Before a blind date, we think about what to wear, where to go, and what to talk about, and prepare our responses. In the same way, we prepare answers to anticipated interview questions. When we fail an interview, it is probably because we did not meet the interviewers’ expectations. Both blind dating and hiring are fiercely competitive. There are frequent reports lately about how difficult the job market is, but finding a job seems to have always been hard. It might actually have been more concerning if employment were easy to find. Whether it is a job or a blind date, the difficulty naturally calls for a corresponding level of effort. It is not easy to find a relationship from a single blind date. Likewise, do not be too discouraged if you do not receive a final job offer. One way to improve your chances of finding a relationship is to go on more blind dates, and hiring is similar. Submit as many résumés as you can, keep reflecting on your experiences, and work toward finding a company that fits you. In one sentence: Become the person the other side is looking for.

title: No Matter How Far Artificial Intelligence Advances
description: While browsing the web today, I happened to read an interesting post. Many people have already discussed similar themes, but every new version of ChatGPT brings predictions of jobs being replaced and makes countless workers afraid…
content: ※ This post was carried over when I moved my blog. (Originally written: November 12, 2024) While browsing the web today, I happened to read an interesting post . Many people have probably already discussed similar themes over and over. It may feel repetitive, but every new version of ChatGPT brings claims that it will replace many occupations, leaving countless workers afraid. It is an unfortunate reality, but one we have to accept. [\[AI for Everyone\] Part 1 — The Past and Present of Artificial Intelligence, Now Well Past Sixty (The Dong A Ilbo)](https://www.donga.com/news/It/article/all/20220608/113851410/1) The concept and term "artificial intelligence" were established about 68 years ago, but I think the arrival of ChatGPT opened the AI era. We are living through the transition from the information age to the age of artificial intelligence. I don't know what the atmosphere was like during the dot com bubble or the first arrival of smartphones, but I imagine now might feel similar. I think AI will naturally become part of our lives, and it is already used in many aspects of everyday life. Recently, I called a bank's customer service center, and an AI agent was handling the work. Even a visit to a café or restaurant shows how common it has become to order through a kiosk rather than a person. To survive in a rapidly changing era, we also need the ability to adapt quickly. The ultimate goal of every technological advance is to improve human quality of life, and most inventions can be understood as extensions of the human body. AI has begun entering the domain of the brain, where we think, and is trying to reach into the heart as well. In other words, as time passes, machines may be able to replace every physical activity humans can perform. Simple labor and repetitive tasks will be the easiest to replace first. Personally, I think even professions such as doctors, judges, and lawyers could someday be replaced by AI. Even so, as the title of this post suggests, if there are areas that AI can never reach no matter how far it advances, they are responsibility, ethics, and curiosity. Believing in what we cannot see, imagining it, and creating it are uniquely human abilities.

title: My IELTS Test Experience
description: I took IELTS on Saturday, October 12, and received my results by email around 9 p.m. on Sunday the 13th. I was surprised by how quickly they arrived. Although I did not reach my target score, I am satisfied with the result of my first English test. Above all, I learned a lot while preparing…
content: ※ This post was moved from my previous blog during a migration. (Originally written: October 26, 2024) I took IELTS on Saturday, October 12, and received my results by email around 9 p.m. on Sunday the 13th. I was surprised by how quickly they arrived. Although I did not reach my target score, I am satisfied with the result of my first English test. Above all, I picked up a lot of information while preparing, and I am writing this belated reflection to record it. (Addendum: After finishing, I realized this feels more like a review than a reflection. Next time, I should try to write a proper reflection.) What is IELTS? IELTS (International English Language Testing System) is an internationally recognized test of English proficiency. It consists of four sections: Listening / Reading / Writing / Speaking . Listening (40 minutes), Reading (one hour), and Writing (one hour) run consecutively without a break for a total of two hours and 40 minutes. Speaking is held separately and takes about 12–14 minutes. You can choose between General Training / Academic , and between computer based and paper based testing. Choosing the test type, format, and venue Unlike TOEIC, IELTS is not limited to a fixed regular schedule; you can take it whenever a place is available. Check availability and register on the official IDP website. I recommend booking at least a week in advance. Registration requires passport details, so obtain a passport beforehand. I chose General Training on computer and booked an afternoon session at IDP’s Gangbuk location in Nambuk Square. Some people struggle to choose the test type and format. For the type, choose according to your purpose—for example, Academic for graduate school or General Training for immigration. The format is simply a matter of preference. I chose computer based testing because I am comfortable typing, and I felt each format had its own pros and cons. It also seems best to study in conditions as close to the actual test environment as possible. Unfortunately, it did not feel appropriate to take photos at the venue, so I did not. It was not far from the station and was easy to reach by public transit. The test center was on the building’s 20th floor and felt like a rented section of the building. It was rather small—about 20 people would fill it—but the facilities were clean. As this was my first IELTS test, I had no other venue to compare it with, but I experienced no particular inconvenience. I have, however, read other reviews mentioning noise during the test. If you have lunch nearby, I recommend the chicken set meal at “Sarangbang Kalguksu,” close to the test center. With good prices, good food, and seating for solo diners, it should be very satisfying. The test experience Speaking The speaking test lasts about 12–14 minutes and has three parts. Part 1 is a basic conversation. In Part 2, you receive a prompt, have one minute to prepare, and then speak in English on your own. Part 3 is a more in depth conversation based on what you discussed in Part 2. When preparing, I found speaking difficult to study because I had no one to talk to. I used italki, a platform for one on one online English lessons, but the cost can be a burden. While looking for study methods, I found a free option I recommend: joining the IELTS Prep Discord. It is a channel with IELTS candidates from around the world, where you can find a speaking partner and practice in real time. It is free, and speaking with people from other countries feels somewhat like talking to an actual examiner, which is great. My test was at 11:40, and these were the questions I actually received. Part 1 Q: Do you live in a city or a town? (What is the difference between the two…?) Q: What are the advantages of where you live? Why? Q: Is there somewhere near where you live that you would recommend? Why? Q: Do you like taking photos? Why? Part 2 & Part 3 Q: Talk about an experience when you helped family or friends. What happened? Who did you help, and what did you do? What was I doing at that moment? Why did you do it? The very first question in Part 1 threw me off a little. I wondered whether “city” and “town” were different, but felt I had to answer, so I responded quickly. After that, I think things went smoothly. When I received the Part 2 prompt, it was fascinating to see what I had watched in YouTube videos happening right in front of me. I do not remember the Part 3 questions very well. I may have given some unexpected answers, but I do not think I got stuck on any of the examiner’s questions. It was my first time ever speaking face to face with a foreigner, so I was very nervous. The test took place in a very relaxed atmosphere, and I never felt interrupted or treated rudely. Listening, Reading, Writing The test proceeds in the order Listening, Reading, Writing. Be sure to remember that there are no breaks between them. The total test time is almost three hours, so it is more tiring than expected, and concentrating for that long is not easy. When preparing, it may help to get into the habit of completing the sections consecutively. I prepared using only The Official Cambridge Guide to IELTS, Cambridge IELTS books 15–19, and a Hackers vocabulary book. I chose them because they are the best known and are used by most academies. Having taken the test, I think they were definitely helpful. You can find good explanations of the question types in each IELTS section on YouTube. Working through many questions to get a feel for them matters, but it also helps to know the formats beforehand, so set aside time to familiarize yourself with the question types. Knowing plenty of vocabulary is certainly useful, and knowing many synonyms is especially helpful when answering questions. For reference, the Cambridge books are essentially practice test books containing past exam questions, and they are expensive at KRW 34,000. You can buy them cheaply secondhand or easily find PDFs through an internet search. Conclusion Preparing for IELTS reduced some of my fear of English, which I had always assumed would be difficult. I think this test is more practical than other English certification exams. During preparation, I gradually learned how to study English and changed my surroundings to make it easier to encounter the language. As you study, you notice that English is used in many parts of daily life. I also think our level of education has risen enough that we can communicate with foreigners without much difficulty. Still, the English we commonly use is only at a fairly basic level. To learn a language, you need plenty of exposure and familiarity. I do not know whether I will take IELTS again, but I think steady effort will lead to better results.

title: Do You Know Korea?
description: The image above brings together people and works that have introduced Korea to the world and, as we say, enhanced its national prestige. We often call this the “Do You Know Club,” a meme about figures foreigners recognize when asked “Do you know Korea?”…
content: ※ This post was carried over when I moved my blog. (Originally written: October 23, 2024) The Do You Know Club The image above brings together people and works that have introduced Korea to the world and, as we say, enhanced its national prestige. We often call this the "Do You Know Club." It began as a meme: people who raised Korea's profile enough for foreigners to recognize it when asked "Do you know Korea?" should be inducted into the Do You Know Club . At first, most members were world famous athletes such as Park Ji sung and Kim Yuna, but now it includes many idols and artists, including PSY and BTS. In the past, global events held every four years, such as the Olympics and the World Cup, were the main stages for bringing honor to the country. The state would offer benefits such as prize money to citizens who achieved that. These days, however, there are more ways to raise Korea's standing beyond traditional sports, including esports, television dramas, and music. This has sparked controversy over special military service treatment. The principles and criteria for enhancing national prestige are ambiguous, and the concept has lost much of its old meaning. In fact, many Koreans are making Korea known across a wide range of fields, and articles about international recognition for Korea have been appearing frequently. In this post, let's look at some representative examples. K Literature Recently, news that Korean author Han Kang had won the Nobel Prize in Literature came as a major surprise to many people. It was especially meaningful as the second Nobel Prize awarded to a Korean, after the Peace Prize, and Korea's first Nobel Prize in Literature. It was also the first award to an Asian in the literature category. Han Kang's Nobel winning work, "Human Acts," sold out around the world and has attracted great interest among readers both in Korea and abroad. Yet before she won the Nobel Prize, some people claimed her work contained historical distortions, and the book was even designated harmful reading. Her winning the Nobel Prize despite that surprised many and demonstrated that Korean literature had received recognition overseas. There have recently been frequent reports about declining reading among Koreans. Against that backdrop, the Nobel news rekindled people's desire to read. Receiving such an award in the month of Hangeul Day, and in autumn—a good season for reading—made it all the more meaningful. K POP Two days ago, Rosé released "APT," a new collaboration with Bruno Mars. It is Rosé's first solo song since BLACKPINK disbanded, and it has attracted enormous attention, reaching 40 million YouTube views within two days of its release. (At the time of writing, it is approaching 100 million views.) Just three months earlier, Bruno Mars worked with Lady Gaga on "Die With A Smile," which is currently at No. 5 on the Billboard chart and receiving a lot of love. Bruno Mars has also produced enduring hits such as "Uptown Funk" and "Nothin' On You," and is popular worldwide as a singer representing South America. I think a singer at that level collaborating with a Korean idol shows just how much the standing of K pop culture has grown. I see this as the result of Korean idol culture, which began in the 1990s, being refined over time. People often say we are now in the fourth generation of Korean idols, and today's idols in particular are collaborating with global pop stars. Examples include SEVENTEEN and DJ Khaled, BTS and Coldplay, BLACKPINK and Selena Gomez, and BTS's Jungkook and Charlie Puth. These artists' fandoms extend around the world, and the entertainment industry is making the greatest contribution to promoting Korea. K Beauty K pop and Korean dramas have captured the hearts of many overseas fans, and beauty and fashion have probably benefited the most. You can see this in the destinations foreign tourists frequent. If I had to name the streets most visited by foreigners since COVID 19, I'd choose Myeongdong and Seongsu dong. Myeongdong, packed with cosmetics stores, and Seongsu dong, now called the leading fashion district among young people, have become their favorite hot spots. Also, iHerb, the online store where people can buy supplements and health foods directly from overseas, has a "K Beauty" category. Sunscreen from the Korean cosmetics brand Beauty of Joseon is a bestseller there. A YouTube search easily turns up videos of foreigners reviewing these products. Meanwhile, plastic surgery is attracting considerable attention as well. The number of foreigners visiting Korea for cosmetic procedures has risen sharply, and brokers helping arrange surgery trips have reportedly emerged. Korean plastic surgery techniques have thus become widely known overseas and are helping shape Korea's image. K Food "Culinary Class Wars," one of the most popular series on Netflix these days, features a variety of chefs competing in cooking challenges. (Although I haven't watched it yet,) the program presents not just Korean food but a range of dishes reflecting each chef's personality. Chef Jung Ji sun's baisi, showcased as part of her Chinese cooking, drew great interest even among Chinese viewers. Some tourists reportedly come from overseas to visit restaurants run by chefs who appeared on the show. Spicy food challenges have also become popular among young people through social media, and Buldak spicy noodles have been a major hit overseas. There's a strong impression that Koreans handle spicy food well, probably stemming from bright red kimchi. An indispensable part of the Korean table, kimchi is soul food for Koreans and one of the first Korean foods foreigners think of. "Do you know kimchi?" used to be a common opening when introducing Korea, but perceptions have changed so much that the phrase now feels a little dated. Conclusion So far, we've looked at Korea's K culture. From the examples above alone, it is clear that the world recognizes Koreans. Yet we call our own country "Hell Joseon." How ironic. Seen through foreigners' eyes, Korea is clearly a very good place to live. But many online communities are full of people saying Korea has no future, casually claiming that "the smarter you are, the sooner you leave Korea," encouraging emigration or international marriage, and busily tearing one another down. When did it become like this? I don't know why, but it isn't a situation where we can simply blame someone. I remember residents gathering in our apartment complex to cheer during the 2002 World Cup when I was young, and the entire complex erupting in a simultaneous roar whenever a goal was scored. Today, however, people react sensitively even to small noises such as dogs barking or babies walking, and complaints about noise between apartments are frequent. In elementary school, I learned to care for vulnerable people such as older adults, people with disabilities, and pregnant women. Now I feel not only that respect for older people is disappearing, but that attitudes are turning toward dismissing them or treating them with hostility. Although I haven't lived all that long, comparing Korea now with just twenty years ago shows how rapidly it has changed. Individual dispositions, daily habits, spending patterns, and even culture have all shifted. Whether these changes are positive or negative depends, I think, on each person's interpretation. Many things may change in the future too, but when we don't even know what tomorrow will bring, predicting Korea twenty years from now is incredibly difficult. Still, if there is one thing that does not change amid this upheaval, it is the fact that we are Korean. Being Korean is an inherent characteristic we naturally acquire at birth and cannot change. From that perspective, I hope we at least hold on to our pride in being Korean. In Korea, being Korean may seem extremely common and ordinary, but broaden your view to a global perspective and Koreans are a minority ethnic group with influence far greater than the size of their small territory. So I hope we no longer feel ashamed of being Korean. I hope we refrain from living in Korea while insulting it, which is like lying on your back and spitting upward. At least while reading this post, I hope you felt a surge of national pride.

title: An Old Thought
description: Lately, I’ve often felt that society is becoming sick.
content: ※ This post was carried over when I moved my blog. (Originally written: July 13, 2024, 00:16) Lately, I've often felt that society is becoming sick. Whichever online community, news outlet, or YouTube channel I visit, I frequently see people fighting. Common topics include real estate, politics, the birth rate, gender conflict, and employment, along with claims that Korea will soon collapse. Just a few years ago, livestreamers were making provocative content and tearing each other down for attention. Now that has become a whole genre known as "rekka"—online drama chasers. On AfreecaTV, viewers who excessively adore and defend female streamers are called "water buffaloes." (Learning why might give you the chills.) Another expression used to describe Koreans is "pot mentality" —heating up quickly and cooling down just as fast. I think those two tendencies, together with Instagram and its culture of showing off , are damaging much of Korean culture today. Maybe people have been trapped in the online world since COVID 19... or maybe they've been steeped in dopamine. Either way, people seem angrier. And there's far too much interference in other people's affairs. Judging by the stories that have been appearing in the news lately, gender conflict and birth rate issues will intensify, and conflicts between older and younger people will emerge as well. People of every age and gender divide each other into camps, flock to one side, then get swept over to the other. That's the reality of our country today. As men and women, young and old, all find themselves opposed to one another, Korea inevitably becomes more individualistic. We tend to think of neighboring Japan—the country we so often dislike and treat as an adversary—as highly individualistic. But lately, Korea has become just as individualistic, and increasingly materialistic as well. After thinking carefully about the mindset that might help me survive this chaos, I think there are two things worth keeping in mind. 1\. Take an impossible to argue with attitude: "Yes, it's because I'm stupid. It's because I didn't know any better. It's because I'm too nice." 2\. Don't give power to a jerk. In other words, don't become one yourself. Don't act like a big shot.

title: Small Things Add Up to Something Big
description: I bite my nails when I’m anxious. It’s a childhood habit I still haven’t broken—or perhaps haven’t actively tried to break. The saying that a habit learned at three lasts until eighty came to mind, and from this moment on, I want to change my bad habits…
content: ※ This post was carried over when I moved my blog. (Originally written: July 13, 2024, 00:16) I bite my nails when I'm anxious. It's a habit I've had since childhood, and I still haven't broken it. No—come to think of it, I don't think I've even actively tried. The saying that a habit learned at three lasts until eighty popped into my head, and from the moment I write this, I want to start changing my bad habits. 1\. My actions and thoughts come from who I was in the past. If I stayed up all last night, I'll be tired today. The reason I can't speak English properly now is that I didn't study it ten years ago. This isn't about assigning blame for what I didn't do or can't do. It's simply that I can't do it because I haven't done it. 2\. Biting my nails, crossing my legs when I sit, lying down as soon as I get home, immediately opening social media on public transport—these unconscious behaviors shape me. Why do these bad habits keep staying with me? Because even though I knew they were bad, I didn't make an effort to change them. Without that effort, they became ingrained and remained unconscious habits. 3\. Things we do unconsciously don't consume emotional energy. Emotion will be one of the last uniquely human forms of dignity left in the AI era. That's why we should live with gratitude for being able to feel emotions at all. 4\. We also need to notice the small emotions that come from small actions. Instead of expecting myself to know two things tomorrow because I learned one today, if I thank myself for making it possible to learn that one thing today, I'll unconsciously keep doing something consistently and eventually reach a hundred. 5\. You can't start at a hundred from the beginning. 6\. Small things add up to something big.

title: When You Shouldn’t Scrimp
description: Money isn’t everything in life. And listening to various wealthy people, it seems that having a lot of it doesn’t necessarily make you happy.
content: ※ This post was carried over when I moved my blog. (Originally written: July 9, 2024, 12:50) Money isn't everything in life. And listening to various wealthy people, it seems that having a lot of it doesn't necessarily make you happy. Still, one definite advantage of having money is that it gives you more choices. We've all probably had the experience of wanting to buy something and thinking, ' Ah... I'd rather buy B than A, but I don't have the money... ' It feels as though money would solve everything, but because we don't have it right now, we want to use what we do have as efficiently as possible. Yet there are moments in life when we shouldn't scrimp. They involve things inseparable from our lives and closely tied to money: what we commonly call clothing, food, and shelter . They're all important, but food is one area people quietly tend to neglect. Personally, I don't think we should judge what we eat solely by how much we get for our money. https://post.naver.com/viewer/postView.naver?volumeNo=32642787 In Korea's entrenched culture of showing off, there are young people who can't afford a home but drive sports cars while eating convenience store food every day. I think this is another bad habit created by Instagram. For starters, I really dislike the culture of showing off. Cars, watches, and things like that are luxuries, and you can live perfectly well without them. Anyway, saying not to judge food solely by value for money doesn't mean I'm telling you not to visit omakase or Michelin starred restaurants to take photos. Places like omakase and Michelin restaurants are expensive partly because of the atmosphere, but also because they operate by reservation and use fresh, high quality ingredients. These days, with Coupang Rocket Fresh deliveries working so well and recipes available for anything you search on YouTube, cooking for yourself is the healthiest way to eat—as long as you can be bothered. People today are said to enjoy eating out because cooking and cleaning up take so much time. And as inflation pushes restaurant prices higher, people increasingly look for cheap options, including frozen food and inexpensive eateries. Food goes directly into our bodies, so it is directly connected to our health. https://www.mk.co.kr/news/society/11060486 Suspected food poisoning affects over 1,000 people at 24 schools… Kimchi throws Namwon into turmoil — Maeil Business Newspaper If you walk into a restaurant and its hygiene looks questionable, I recommend getting out without looking back... This seems especially, especially important in summer. Conclusion: Don't scrimp on what you eat.

title: Beware of Scammers, Anytime and Anywhere
description: To survive in an unforgiving Korea, you have to watch out for scams that could happen anytime and anywhere.
content: ※ This post was carried over when I moved my blog. (Originally written: July 3, 2024, 17:49) To survive in an unforgiving Korea, you have to watch out for scams that could happen anytime and anywhere. https://www.newsis.com/view/NISX20240701 0002794401 All kinds of incidents happen everywhere, every day, but I think the issue making headlines lately is jeonse fraud involving large housing deposits. It's especially heartbreaking because most of the victims are young people just starting their working lives. Some landlords—the people renting out the homes—even claim it was an accident or disaster, not fraud. I found that pretty absurd. I think jeonse fraud is a somewhat special case, and because scammers approach you with a plan from the beginning, you can still fall victim even if you're on guard. Voice phishing is a typical example. So there are two things worth remembering to protect yourself from scams. 1\. Be wary of people who are especially nice to you when you've just met. On that subject, I once heard that there's only a paper thin line between a scammer and a businessperson. 2\. If they follow through on what they say, they're a businessperson. If they ultimately fail to keep their word, they're a scammer. Recently, I joined the social platform Threads to bring traffic to my blog and began posting summaries of my articles. I saw lots of people I'd never come across on Twitter or Telegram before, and just as I was thinking, "There really are a lot of skilled people out there," I found an account that seemed like a scammer's. This industry already has a reputation for being full of scammers, and I thought accounts like this would only reinforce that impression, so I'm writing this to leave a permanent record on my blog. They had been posting screenshots boasting of profits on Threads and charging people to enter their open KakaoTalk chatroom. 6/14 — Called out an impersonator and declared, "Imitate, don't copy and paste." 6/25 — Posted an ETF market overview and chart analysis, but the chart had been stolen from a trader named SASUKE. 6/30 — When caught, they blocked the person who confronted them and deleted the post, perhaps out of embarrassment. This is someone who doesn't know how to keep their own word. Therefore, they're a scammer. Even if they aren't a scammer yet, they're well on their way to becoming a textbook example. If it was a misunderstanding, clear it up. If you did something wrong, say you're sorry. You only have to say it once, but scammers seem to find that difficult because of their needless pride. 1. Screenshots proving profits can all be fabricated, so don't be dazzled into trusting them too much. 2. Even if there are plenty of testimonials from followers, those can all be fabricated too, so don't trust them. 3. There is absolutely no magical technique that instantly puts you in the fast lane to wealth.

title: What Does Korea Need to Revitalize Its Blockchain Industry?
description: In Korea, the public is probably still more familiar with the word crypto than blockchain. And when people hear crypto, the response is often, 'Isn’t that a scam?' That is both a problem and the reality of this market…
content: In Korea, the public is probably still more familiar with the word crypto than blockchain. And when people hear “crypto,” the response is often, “Isn’t that a scam?” That is both a problem and the reality of this market. I imagine things are similar in other countries, too, although I have never been abroad, so I cannot say for sure. While recently searching for information on the Virtual Asset User Protection Act, I came across articles about struggling exchanges shutting down one after another. Regulations are also being reviewed and advanced rapidly on several other fronts, including suspending exchange reviews when major shareholders are under investigation and banning relevant Ministry of Justice employees from holding crypto. Quite literally, running a blockchain business in Korea has become more difficult. Personally, I see these government interventions as very positive measures that could help prevent events like FTX’s bankruptcy or the Mt. Gox hack. Crypto only exchange closures accelerate… Qubit announces the end of its service There are various blockchain businesses in Korea today. To look at a few categories, exchanges are represented by the familiar big five: Upbit, Bithumb, Korbit, Coinone, and GOPAX. Exchanges and businesses managing virtual asset operations are classified as virtual asset service providers and must comply with the revised Virtual Asset User Protection Act. Businesses outside that group, meanwhile, are generally classified under information and communications, specifically software development and supply. Blockchain networks are one example. Names representing Korea include Luna, which has unfortunately already fallen, Klaytn, Wemade, Finschia (formerly LINK), and others such as Orbit Chain and Kroma (WEMIX Canvas). I do not know exactly why, but once a project issues a coin, public perceptions often turn negative. By contrast, infrastructure—nodes—is an area with businesses that have remained relatively solid in Korea, earned global recognition, and continued operating steadily. DSRV, A41, and Cosmostation belong to this category. Marketing and research also seem to have endured. Xangle, DeSpread, Four Pillars, and Coinness come to mind. There were once education providers such as Code States, Like Lion, and Ludium, but they seem to have disappeared now (?). I have listed only the companies that came to mind; there are also companies developing particular dApps and venture investors such as Hashed. How many of these companies are actually earning money entirely through their businesses? There are probably only a handful generating sustainable revenue without issuing tokens. This is likely a problem shared by 95% of blockchain companies worldwide. Even so, what are people focusing on, and what problems are they solving? The year 2024 is different from the ICO days of 2018, when people were selling dreams. “Decentralization” already sounds like an old slogan, and it seems to resonate with no one anymore. After so many painful episodes, including the Luna collapse and FTX’s bankruptcy, the scene has been left largely to veterans. Unlike before, newcomers may become KOLs, traders, or people entering the industry to develop their careers. Whatever their reason for entering this market, they often encounter difficult technology and a high barrier to entry. Personally, I feel the way newcomers encounter that barrier has changed. I am not sure why this is, either. Perhaps it is because AI technology has advanced, or perhaps it reflects a problem in a blockchain market that places more importance on marketing than technology. According to Chainalysis data, understanding of blockchain is low in Korea, while negative perceptions are high. Many Koreans view blockchain negatively because of past events such as Luna’s collapse, Haru Invest, and WEMIX. Stay in this industry long enough, and you realize that even when something is not a scam, once enough people call it one, that becomes its reality. title: Thoughts on Leverage
description: You have probably heard at least once that the stock market is the flower of capitalism.
content: Leverage Rob Moore, Leverage You have probably heard at least once that the stock market is the flower of capitalism. The principle behind stocks is to buy low and sell high. And one of the tools that helps grow your assets is leverage . Margin trading involves borrowing money from a brokerage to buy assets, so it uses leverage. Leverage also brings liquidity to futures markets for relatively low volatility assets such as commodities and financial indexes. However, leveraged positions may be liquidated depending on their expiry date or price. That is why you should never borrow from a bank to trade futures: it compounds your risk. In crypto markets, many people use perpetual futures for margin trading. Because they are not borrowing money from the exchange, they simply lose the money they have put in. With overseas futures, though, you can end up buried in debt… Some people advise against futures because of liquidation risk, while others recommend them. Personally, I think you should trade both futures and spot. There is not really one right answer; I recommend finding and trading what fits your own criteria. When trading futures, you should make the most of leverage. Rather than small scale approaches such as a 1x short hedge to collect funding fees or trading the kimchi premium, I want to introduce two things to watch when actively trading. The most basic approach is to adjust your leverage. 100x or 125x really is gambling—something to try only with money you can afford to lose… No matter how confident you feel, the risk is far too high to make that your strategy. This varies with each person’s judgment, but I usually trade between 2x and 10x. The second important point is strict stop loss management. The reason is to avoid liquidation. If you sit there desperately praying and the market wipes you out in one move, there is no undoing it. You need to respect your stop loss levels more strictly than you would in spot trading. As long as you survive, you may eventually recover, so do everything you can to avoid going to zero. Yesterday, news involving Mt. Gox and Bitcoin’s decline caused one person to lose $12 million. That is roughly KRW 16 billion, lost all at once… They reportedly went all in on Ether. Honestly, I suspect they entered with more than 10x leverage. It is unfortunate, but it seems their own greed brought disastrous consequences. Put aside the thought that “something like this could never happen to me.” I recommend gradually building good trading habits while the amounts are still small… ※ This post was moved from my previous blog during a migration.
